idea.lens: Neuroscience and biological computation: what crosses a cortical cycle boundary is a spike pattern (all-or-none, the readout IS the carried state), and prefrontal working memory is held under a basal-ganglia gate whose default is NoGo (hold exactly) with a learned Go (overwrite). A transformer loop violates both: its carried residual has hundreds of dimensions no loss ever sees, and its memory is append-only.
idea.name: Striatal Frame Loop (SFL): a readout-is-state register cycle for small transformers
idea.one_sentence: Replace the continuous recurrent state of a looped transformer with a fixed-size frame of discrete register slots that is rewritten in place once per short forward pass under hard hold-by-default gates, so that the only object carried from one reasoning step to the next is that step's own argmax readout, exactly as a spike pattern is the only thing one cortical cycle hands to the next.
idea.mechanism: Context layout per cycle t: [rulebook R, N_R tokens, KV-cached once per request] [frame: M slot positions; input embedding at slot m is E[v_m^t] + P_m where v_m^t is a vocabulary token (the slot's current value) and P_m is a fixed per-slot position embedding, i.e. hard addressing by position, no soft content addressing] [one halt/answer position]. Attention: slots attend to R and bidirectionally to all M slots (a frame is a synchronous state, like a CA row); R is causal and cached. One forward pass of a 20M to 60M decoder produces, at every slot m in parallel, value logits z_m in R^V through the ordinary LM head and one gate logit g_m through a 1-dim head. Update rule (hard, no interpolation): v_m^{t+1} = argmax z_m if sigmoid(g_m) > 0.5, else v_m^{t+1} = v_m^t. A held slot is copied bit-exactly; there is no state tensor other than the M integers, so a slot untouched for 10,000 cycles has zero drift by construction. Training signal: the researcher's reference implementations already emit the full state after every step, so each cycle is one supervised transition with loss L = sum_m [BCE(g_m, 1[v_m^{t+1} != v_m^t]) + 1[v_m^{t+1} != v_m^t] * CE(z_m, v_m^{t+1})]; the content loss is applied only where the interpreter's diff says a slot changed, the gate loss is the diff itself. Teacher forcing feeds ground-truth frames, so no gradient ever crosses a cycle boundary: this is local learning in the biological sense, each transition learned from an observed state sequence (the hippocampal-replay analogue is the interpreter trace), and the transition function at cycle 1 and cycle 10,000 sees inputs from the same distribution because every input is a valid frame rather than a drifted vector. A scheduled-sampling phase (feed the model's own argmax frames for a fraction of cycles) closes exposure bias, as in the universal-computer setup. Multi-token values: a slot is F sub-fields (F=4 for integers, F=1 for symbols) predicted in parallel with one gate per slot. Within-frame dependencies: the interpreter's step granularity is chosen so the next frame is a function of the current frame only (one assignment per step for sequential rule systems; synchronous update for CA-like systems), which makes the parallel per-slot prediction exact; where a rule system needs G dependent writes per step, the L layers are split into G blocks with an argmax-and-re-embed snap between blocks, each block locally supervised (the theta-gamma nesting: G serial transitions per theta cycle), which is optional and not part of the killing experiment. Inference: static shape (N_R + M + 1) per request, fixed T cycles or a halt slot that does not change shape, so the whole loop CUDA-graphs on the researcher's H200 profile; per cycle cost is one short forward pass over a few hundred positions with the rulebook KV cached; the context never grows, which is PENCIL's bound obtained for free. Why this differs from the measured +1-step recurrence: in Ouro, looped, ARMT and Coconut the carried object is a residual vector with d degrees of freedom that no per-step loss constrains (the June 2026 readout-blind-spot paper measures final-loop norms drifting to 39,207 at 44M and 56,051 at 129M under per-loop cross-entropy through normalized readouts); token CoT carries only an argmax and extrapolates 60x; SFL carries only an argmax per slot, in parallel, in place, and with an exact hold, so it inherits the token channel's error-correcting reset and local targets while paying one forward pass per step instead of tens of serial decodes per trace line and no context growth.
idea.why_it_could_be_a_breakthrough: Today the belief is that latent serial depth in small models caps near k~4 (Beyond Memorization, Ouro, looped transformers, the researcher's own 0.000 on multi-step composition) and that deep execution therefore requires generating tokens, which is serial wall-clock (Qwen3.5-4B burns ~240M output tokens for AA Index 20). If SFL works, a 20M to 60M "execution cortex" runs prose-specified rule systems invented after training for thousands of steps at roughly one millisecond per step, with a bounded context, exact state, and a per-transition correctness certificate obtainable by enumerating discrete transitions (as Discrete NAR and Cai et al. 2017 did). A 1B knowledge model (the researcher's 350M or MiniCPM5-1B class) then delegates any rule-following computation to the frame by writing the initial slots and reading the answer slot: the cortex/striatum/thalamus split, where knowledge and execution are separate tissues joined by a shared discrete state. Concretely: the universal-computer result (59.5M, 7,552 PENCIL lines, each line tens of serial tokens) would drop from roughly 10^5 serial decode steps to 7,552 short static-shape forward passes, on the order of one second on an H200 at the researcher's measured 34.8% graphed utilization, and the same machine would extend to depths no training run ever saw. It would also settle the open question in the evidence base: the token/latent gap is not about the token modality or about supervision alone; it is about whether hidden degrees of freedom cross the step boundary.
idea.evidence_that_generates_it: (1) Beyond Memorization: token CoT with stepwise supervision >0.90 at k<=4 while GPT-NeoX/ARMT/ACT sit at 0.40 (k=2) and <0.25 (k=3,4) and depth sweeps to 12 layers give only marginal gains; the full paper confirms no variant supervised latent states without tokens and none discretized the carried state, so the decisive cell of the 2x2 (discrete carry, per-step supervision, no serial tokens) has never been run. (2) Universal computer: 59.5M, traces capped at 128 lines, perfect at 7,552 lines, ~60x extrapolation, with PENCIL bounding context by space complexity; the carried object there is an argmax token. (3) Ouro 1.4B: 41.2, 60.4, 66.7, 67.5 then degradation past trained depth; Saunshi 1-layer x 8 loops = 8-layer model (73.2 vs 73.2) and stops; the July 2026 retrofit paper gets ~1.5x extrapolation from per-step-supervised continuous recurrence (70% at depth 18 from support 8, plateau beyond); the June 2026 readout-blind-spot paper shows per-loop CE leaves carried norms drifting to 39,207 and 56,051. Continuous carry with supervision: ~1.5x. Discrete carry with supervision: 60x (tokens) or perfect (Discrete NAR). (4) NLI: removing the discrete program takes 97% to 1%. (5) arXiv 1904.10278: soft addressing degrades exponentially on chained reads; SFL addresses by fixed position and holds by exact copy. (6) Transformers-as-stateless-DNC (2603.19272): the missing pieces are read-modify-write and persistent control state; SFL supplies both as M integers. (7) The researcher's H200 numbers: 10% eager, 34.8% graphed, shapes must be static; SFL is static-shape by design. (8) The researcher's 350M: 0.947 retrieval, 0.680 single-step rule application, 0.000 multi-step under six RL objectives; the reference implementations that verify every answer can also emit every intermediate frame, which is the supervision SFL needs. (9) PENCIL 25M at 97% on 5x5 Einstein where CoT collapses: bounded context matters; SFL's context is bounded by construction. (10) Fast-weight/TTT literature never measures serial depth; SFL sidesteps fast weights entirely by keeping state as tokens at fixed positions. (11) Kimi K3 at 1.8% active and the striatal NoGo default both say the same thing: the cheap operation should be "do nothing to this slot."
idea.nearest_prior_art: Searched with 11 queries and read four arXiv sources; the idea sits in a real but narrow gap and several pieces exist separately. Closest: (a) Discrete Neural Algorithmic Reasoning (Rodionov & Prokhorenkova, ICML 2025, arXiv 2402.11628): forces a GNN processor's carried node/edge states into a finite set, teacher-forced on hint transitions, gets perfect size generalization and provable correctness; ablation shows the processor without discretization performs at baseline level. That is the strongest existing proof that discrete carry plus per-step supervision generalizes. It is per-algorithm, has no program in context, no hard hold gate (every state is re-predicted each step), and is not a language model. (b) Training Transformers as a Universal Computer (arXiv 2604.25166): serial token traces with PENCIL erase, 60x extrapolation; every step costs tens of serial tokens; no parallel frame, no in-place state, no latency discussion. (c) "What I cannot execute, I do not understand" (arXiv 2503.05703): introduces a "dynamic scratchpad", a single self-contained token state rewritten each step, and a "compact scratchpad" that emits only changed variables; both are serial token generation, which is the token-space ancestor of SFL's frame and diff-gate. (d) Emergent Discrete Controller Modules (Rafiuddin & Khan, ICLR 2026): Gumbel-softmax opcode selection with registers inside transformer blocks; registers are continuous with soft addressing and a write intensity lambda, steps happen per layer (depth-bounded), extrapolation 2x to 4x with decay (Sorting 97.4 to 91.6, BFS 95.3 to 83.5). Discrete opcodes, continuous state: the opposite half of SFL. (e) Recurrent Memory Transformer (continuous memory tokens rewritten per segment) and MetaState (arXiv 2603.01331, continuous slots for diffusion LMs): in-place but continuous, no gate. (f) Readout blind spot (arXiv 2606.24898) and Retrofitting Recurrent Depth (arXiv 2608.11233): document the continuous-carry ceiling SFL is built to escape; neither tries a discrete carry. (g) Capabilities and Fundamental Limits of Latent CoT (arXiv 2602.01148) proves argmax acts as an error-correcting reset and latent CoT accumulates compounding error; Discrete Latent Reasoning (arXiv 2606.29712) and Token Assorted (2502.03275) show discrete latent tokens beat continuous ones, but as serial appended tokens with no persistence or overwrite. (h) Models Take Notes at Prefill (arXiv 2606.17107) proposes a "programmable KV cache" and states explicitly that no model has been trained for in-place editing. (i) Cai, Shin, Song 2017: bounded fresh state per recursive call gives provably perfect NPI generalization where the unbounded LSTM state is fragile. (j) Progress Extrapolating Algorithmic Learning (arXiv 2003.08494): activation binning plus digital loss plus localized memory gives 100% extrapolation on Neural GPU tasks, with the observation that a network whose internal state count grows with length cannot extrapolate. (k) Traylor, Merullo, Frank, Pavlick 2024: frontostriatal-style input/output gating emerges in vanilla transformers on the reference-back task; PBWM (O'Reilly & Frank 2006) is the biological model of the gate. (l) A small GitHub demo (gregorycoppola/learner, 2026) trains a 2-layer transformer to predict one-step Turing-machine snapshots with per-cell categorical heads and unrolls it: a toy precedent for parallel discrete frame prediction, without a program in context or a gate. I did not find any work that carries a discrete multi-slot frame in place across forward passes of a decoder with a program in context and a hard, diff-supervised hold gate, nor any matched comparison of continuous versus discrete carry under identical per-step supervision on multi-slot state.
idea.what_is_genuinely_new: Four things. First, the design law and its test: "nothing crosses the step boundary except the readout." The field currently reads the token/latent gap as a supervision story; the June and July 2026 results show per-step supervision of continuous carry still leaves invisible degrees of freedom that drift and caps extrapolation near 1.5x, while the discrete-carry results (universal computer, Discrete NAR) extrapolate 60x or perfectly. Nobody has isolated that variable with matched supervision on a transformer with the program in context; SFL is the architecture that sets it to zero, and the experiment below is the first head-to-head at matched supervision on multi-slot state. Second, the hard hold-by-default gate with bit-exact copy, supervised from the interpreter diff. LSTM/GRU gates interpolate, NTM/DNC erase-and-add is soft, the ICLR 2026 controller writes with a continuous intensity, RMT and MetaState carry continuous vectors, masked diffusion only carries over unmasked tokens and never overwrites; the compact scratchpad predicts diffs but as serial tokens. A hold that is an identity on integers makes persistence a non-learned operation, which is what the KV cache gets right and what every recurrent memory gets wrong, and it is the striatal NoGo default made literal. Third, a decoder LM trained with a mutable region of its own context: M positions at fixed addresses rewritten in place with vocabulary tokens, read through ordinary attention and written through the ordinary LM head, so the same frame is readable by the knowledge model and by a human. The programmable-KV-cache paper names this as future work. Fourth, the claim that the frame turns serial depth into a static-shape loop with O(1) tokens per step and bounded context, which is a wall-clock claim the token-trace line has not made and cannot make. What is not new, stated plainly: discretizing a carried state (Discrete NAR, binning), per-step trace supervision (scratchpad, NPI, CLRS hints), memory tokens (RMT), and the neuroscience mapping of gates to attention (Traylor et al.). SFL's contribution is the specific combination forced by one principle plus the experiment that can kill it.
idea.killing_experiment: Task: the researcher's invented formal systems with reference implementations emitting the full state after each step, plus 1dCA in the Beyond Memorization protocol (disjoint train/test rules) as an anchor. State = M slots (M in {8, 32}) over a vocabulary of 64 to 256 symbols; rulebook in context (100 to 300 tokens); train depth k in [1, 8]; test on held-out rule systems at k in {8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256}. Backbone: one 20M to 60M decoder shared by all arms, identical data, identical per-step supervision, three seeds. Arms: (A) continuous carry, normalized readout (Coconut/looped style: slot residual vectors fed back, per-step CE on decoded slot values); (B) continuous carry with the readout-blind-spot fixes (raw readout or norm penalty), to rule out "it was only scale drift"; (C) discrete carry, every slot re-predicted each cycle, argmax embedding fed back, no gate; (D) full SFL: discrete carry plus hard diff-supervised hold gate; (E) serial token dynamic scratchpad (Nye/2503.05703 style) as the known-good accuracy reference and the latency baseline. Metrics: exact-frame accuracy versus k, per-step accuracy, wall-clock per step, context length. Kill conditions, any one of which ends the idea: (1) C and D fail to beat A and B at k >= 32 (4x trained depth) on M=32; then hidden degrees of freedom were not the problem and the token channel's advantage lies elsewhere (e.g. serial composition within a step), and SFL is dead. (2) D does not beat C on traces where 90% of slots are untouched per step; then the striatal gate is decoration and the neuroscience core collapses to "discretize," which already exists. (3) D matches E in accuracy but needs so many refinement sub-passes for within-frame dependencies that wall-clock per step is not at least 10x below E on the same GPU; then the efficiency claim, which is the breakthrough claim, is dead. (4) Per-transition accuracy of D on held-out rule systems stays below 0.999 after training saturates; then 0.99^256 = 0.076 and the "execution cortex" cannot reach the depths that would change anyone's beliefs, and the general-interpreter claim fails even if the carry claim holds. A positive result looks like: D flat near 1.0 to k=256 on held-out systems, C degrading only via per-step error, A and B collapsing by k=16 to 32, E matching D in accuracy at 20x or more the wall-clock and a growing context.
idea.cost: Data generation runs on the M2 Pro from the existing generators (CPU only). Training: 5 arms x 3 seeds x 2 state sizes = 30 runs at 20M parameters, roughly 1 to 3 GPU-hours each on an L40S at about $1/hour, so $30 to $90 for the decisive sweep; a 60M confirmation of arms C, D, E at the largest M and longest test depth adds about $100 to $200; an optional phase where the 350M fact-free checkpoint reads and writes the frame as a tool on an H200 at about $3/hour adds $200 to $400. Total $350 to $700, ceiling $1,000, about one week of wall-clock including the scheduled-sampling and CUDA-graph latency measurements. Everything runs on one GPU at a time and the training loop is standard teacher-forced cross-entropy, so the Coconut codebase and the existing procedural generators cover most of the engineering.

judges.lens: Novelty (prior-art search: 22 Exa queries across transformer executors, discrete carry in looped transformers, in-place discrete refinement, NAR gating, CA/Turing-machine emulation, in-context memory tokens, neuro-inspired gating)
judges.verdict:
The architecture described as SFL's decisive cell already exists and has been trained, and the matched discrete-versus-continuous comparison the proposal calls "never run" has been run. Three items the generator missed:

1. Papailiopoulos, "SUBLEQ Transformer", round 2 (github.com/anadim/subleq-transformer, March 2026; writeup at dimitrisp.substack.com/p/can-you-train-a-computer; a paper.tex ships in the repo, no arXiv id). A 4.9M-parameter, 6-layer bidirectional transformer over a static 33-position frame (1 PC + 32 memory cells, byte vocabulary). The SUBLEQ program lives in those cells, so the program is in context. Trained on single-step interpreter transitions with weighted cross-entropy, 100x on changed positions and 1x on unchanged, which is a soft form of SFL's diff-supervised loss. Inference is argmax per cell, rewritten in place, one forward pass per instruction, fixed shape. Result: 100% single-step on held-out states, and multi-step rollouts on programs never seen as full executions: Fibonacci 47 steps 100%, isqrt 61 steps 95%, division 91 steps 93.8%, 99.8% over 804 programs. Trained in 4 hours on a laptop. That is arm C plus most of arm D plus the static-shape wall-clock property, at the exact scale SFL proposes, with a Turing-complete instruction set. Missing relative to SFL: a separate gate head with bit-exact hold (every cell is re-predicted), and a rulebook for held-out rule systems (the ISA is fixed).

2. Altabaa, Chen, Lafferty, Yang, arXiv 2510.14095 (Oct 2025, revised Aug 2026), "Recursive Latent Space Reasoning". A recurrent transformer with the computation graph (the program) in context, per-node value states, per-iteration algorithmic supervision, and an explicit "discretize and re-embed" step between iterations (their mechanism iii, appendix B.3), plus a noise-injection error-correction mechanism. Perfect generalization from 32-node training graphs to 128-node test graphs, with ablations against feedforward and continuous recurrent baselines under the same supervision. This is the "decisive cell of the 2x2" the proposal says nobody has run: discrete carry, per-step supervision, no serial tokens, program in context, multi-slot state, matched against continuous carry.

3. The hold-by-default gate has direct ancestors. Ibarz et al., arXiv 2209.11142 (Generalist Neural Algorithmic Learner) add an update gate to the processor whose bias initializes it toward not updating node states, the NoGo default in NAR form (soft sigmoid, not bit-exact). Thakkar et al., arXiv 2609.02046 (sparse residual world models) use a per-object change gate plus a delta head that "copies the rest verbatim" and report that the entire win comes from error suppression on the static majority, which is exactly what SFL's kill condition 2 would measure. Mask-Predict (Ghazvininejad 2019) and Lee et al. 2018 are in-place discrete re-prediction with confidence-based hold; Reflective Masking and Self-aware Markov Models (arXiv 2603.16661) add a learned per-position keep/rewrite head and a learned stop head on a discrete canvas, 95% on Sudoku-Extreme.

Further occupied ground: Neural Execution Engines (arXiv 2006.08084) fed binary discrete outputs back into a transformer with learned conditional masking and got near-perfect length generalization on sort/Dijkstra/Prim in 2020. DiscoLoop (arXiv 2607.00341) loops discrete embeddings instead of hidden states. Supervised Thinking States (arXiv 2602.08332) re-embeds teacher-forced tokens and extrapolates on state tracking. Discrete-Valued Neural Communication (arXiv 2107.02367) established discretized inter-step communication as a generalization bias. Zhang, arXiv 2605.30757, already formalizes "full sequence-state loops" versus compressed latent loops as the memory-budget distinction SFL relies on. The Percepta transformer-vm and Coppola's learner repo are further constructed or toy versions of state-in-tokens looping.

The neuroscience framing (spike pattern as carried state, striatal NoGo default) is a new label on these parts, not a new mechanism. Traylor/Soni et al. (arXiv 2402.08211) already mapped frontostriatal gating onto transformers.
judges.strongest_objection: The proposal's central claim, that no one has carried a discrete multi-slot frame in place across forward passes of a small transformer with the program in context and per-step interpreter supervision, is false as of March 2026: the SUBLEQ round-2 model is that object at 4.9M parameters, trained with a changed-position-weighted loss, rolling out 61 to 91 consecutive correct steps on unseen programs from a static 33-position frame. Combined with Altabaa et al. (2510.14095), which already ran the discretize-versus-continuous recurrence ablation under matched algorithmic supervision with the program in context, the killing experiment's arms A/B versus C have a known answer before a single GPU-hour is spent. What remains of SFL is one extra head (the hard hold gate) whose expected effect, error suppression on untouched slots, was just measured in 2609.02046 and found to be the whole story. That is a modest ablation on someone else's architecture, not a breakthrough.
judges.what_survives: Two narrow questions are still open and cheap to test on the researcher's setup. First, rule-system generalization: SUBLEQ has a fixed ISA, Altabaa a fixed operator set, and Beyond Memorization infers the rule from a trajectory rather than reading it; no frame executor has been shown to read a rulebook from context and execute a system invented after training for hundreds of steps. That is the one experiment the researcher's procedural generators make uniquely possible, and it is where the 0.000 multi-step result lives. Second, the exact-hold gate at long horizons: whether bit-exact copy of untouched slots (versus re-predicting all 32 at ~0.999 each, which compounds to failure around 32 slots x 256 steps) is what carries a frame executor from ~100 to ~1000 steps, measured on traces where 90% of slots are static. If both come out positive, the honest framing is "extending Papailiopoulos-style frame execution to in-context rulebooks, with an exact hold gate," cited as such. The wall-clock comparison against PENCIL-style token traces and the within-step dependent-write blocks are worth reporting alongside but do not carry novelty on their own.

judges.verdict:
Source checks. Beyond Memorization (2508.16745, arXiv html) confirms k=1 0.95, k=2 0.40, CoT >0.90 at k<=4, and confirms the 2x2 gap the idea rests on: no variant fed back a discretized state non-autoregressively or supervised latent intermediates without tokens. But the task is rule inference from a 10-state, 20-cell sequence, not rule reading from a rulebook, and the paper says one- and two-step accuracy saturates after 4-6 layers with only marginal gains from width. Universal computer (2604.25166) confirms 59.5M, 128-line cap, 7,552 lines, 100% on multiplication and 100% on SAT over 172,251 lines, token-by-token generation, fixed MicroPy semantics; tokens per line are not reported, so "10^5 serial decodes" is an estimate. Readout blind spot (2606.24898, Sharma and Vu) exists and reports norms in the thousands to tens of thousands at 44M and 129M; the exact 39,207 and 56,051 were not checkable from the abstract. Retrofit (2608.11233, Shapiro) exists and reports 1.5x extrapolation with 70% through depth 18, but training depth is about 12, not the "support 8" the idea states, and it is August, not July. Discrete NAR (2402.11628) is real, ICML 2025, perfect test scores with provable correctness; the "without discretization drops to baseline" ablation is not in the abstract. "What I cannot execute" (2503.05703) is real and already shows a self-contained state rewritten each step working to 14k execution steps in token space; the "compact scratchpad" was not confirmed. "Models Take Notes at Prefill" (2606.17107) uses neither the phrase "programmable KV cache" nor the statement that no model has been trained for in-place editing, so that prior-art line is overclaimed. The repo's compose generator emits per-step running values; the invented-formal-system generators are not in this repo, so "already emit the full state after every step" is unverified.

Consistency with the base. Nothing verified contradicts the carry claim itself: Ouro's degradation past trained depth, the readout blind spot, the 1.5x plateau, Saunshi's loop-equals-deep-model ceiling, and MicroPy's 60x with an argmax carry all sit where the generator puts them. Three places where the evidence does not point where the idea says. (1) NLI's 97 to 1 is about a discrete program, not a discrete carried state; it does not bear on the step-boundary principle. (2) The idea cites the 350M's 0.947/0.680/0.000 as support and omits the same model's in-context anomaly (0.0283 in context vs 0.1233 retrieved, well-formedness 0.34), which is the only measured rulebook-in-context case in the base and it went the wrong way. MicroPy is the counter-example, but only for a fixed formal language trained from scratch. (3) The breakthrough paragraph says "prose-specified rule systems"; the only prose-specified single-step number in the base is 0.680, and the killing experiment quietly switches to formal rulebooks of 100-300 tokens. The formal version is supported; the prose version is contradicted.

Mechanism coherence. Shapes, caching, static graph, and the teacher-forced transition loss are concrete. Two flaws. First, content CE is applied only where the diff says a slot changed, so the LM head at held slots is never trained to reproduce the current value; a gate false positive then writes an untrained argmax into state. With 32 slots and 256 steps that is 8,192 gate decisions per trajectory, so per-slot gate error must sit below about 1e-4. Supervising the content head at every slot with target = next value fixes this at zero cost. Second, "identical per-step supervision" across arms A to D is not achievable as written: a continuous residual cannot be teacher-forced, so A and B must train through their own carried state while C and D train on i.i.d. ground-truth transitions. The comparison confounds "discrete carry" with "teacher-forceable training", so kill condition 1 cannot deliver the interpretation assigned to it, and the headline novelty claim rests on that isolation. Also missed in the prior-art search: Levenshtein Transformer and Mask-Predict rewrite a discrete sequence in place across passes with a per-position keep decision, which is the hold gate applied to a state frame.

Cost and hardware claims are consistent with the base: 30 runs at 20M for $30 to $90, static shapes matching the 34.8% graphed profile. "About one second for 7,552 passes" is optimistic by a few x for launch-bound 20-60M models (0.3 to 1 ms per graphed pass gives 2 to 8 s); the 10x to 20x ratio against W tokens per step is plausible since both sides are launch-bound.
judges.strongest_objection: SFL's per-cycle operation is exactly the k=1 "apply a held-out rule once" task, and the idea declares anything below 0.999 per transition fatal. Every verified k=1 number on held-out rules is far below that: 0.95 in Beyond Memorization, where one-step accuracy saturates after 4-6 layers with only marginal gains from width, and 0.680 for the researcher's own 350M on prose-specified systems. Token CoT >0.90 at k=4 implies per-step application near 0.97 to 0.99 conditional on correct rule inference, still short. The only per-step number above 0.999 in the base (MicroPy, 100% over 172,251 lines, about 1 minus 6e-6 per line) was obtained with fixed interpreter semantics and serial token generation inside each line, so it supports neither held-out rule systems nor the one-pass parallel transition. The discrete carry and hold gate remove drift, but drift never set the per-step number; SFL multiplies whatever per-step error exists 256 times, and on the 1dCA anchor the errors are dominated by rule inference and correlated across cycles, so kill condition 4 as written cannot distinguish a rule-inference failure from a carry failure.
judges.what_survives: The narrow, formal-rulebook version: a 20M to 60M decoder that predicts a discrete state frame in place in one pass per step, trained on teacher-forced transitions, compared against argmax re-prediction without a gate (C) and the serial token scratchpad (E) on the researcher's invented systems with explicit rulebooks. The 2x2 gap is real (Beyond Memorization confirms no discrete-feedback or latent-supervised variant), the bounded-context static-shape loop is real and cheap, and the wall-clock ratio against W tokens per step is measurable for about $100. Required changes: supervise the content head at every slot with target = next value so gate false positives are harmless; give the rule explicitly on the 1dCA anchor or report per-transition accuracy conditioned on correct rule inference; replace the unachievable matched-supervision claim with a teacher-forceable continuous arm (carry the softmax-weighted embedding E^T softmax(z), feed ground-truth one-hot embeddings during training) so hard versus soft carry is isolated from training regime; drop "prose-specified" from the claim until a per-step number above 0.68 exists for prose rules; cite Levenshtein/Mask-Predict as the ancestor of the hold gate. The MicroPy latency claim survives as "fewer launch-bound passes per line", not "one second".

judges.lens: Testability: can the killing experiment be run for under $2,000 on one GPU by one person, is the falsifier a number, and would a positive result change beliefs
judges.verdict:
Runnable at budget, but the decisive arm is confounded and near-certain to pass, while the risky arm most likely fails for a reason unrelated to the architecture.

Cost: the dollar estimate holds. A 20M decoder at 350 positions (100-300 rulebook tokens plus 32 slots plus a halt position) at batch 64 is about 2.7 TFLOPs per step; on an L40S at 30% utilization that is roughly 0.05 s/step, so 50k steps is under an hour and the 1-3 GPU-hour per run figure is generous. Thirty runs plus a 60M confirmation is $100-$400 in GPU time; $1,000 with debugging reruns. Teacher-forced training makes each example a single transition, so data is tiny and generation runs on the M2 Pro. Wall-clock per step under CUDA graphs is a measurement the researcher has already done once (34.8% graphed). The dollars are not the constraint.

The engineering is understated. I read the repo. The Coconut backbone (src/model.py, Block.forward) hard-codes a causal tril mask; SFL needs a bidirectional block over the frame with a causal, cached rulebook, so the attention mask, the KV handling (the frame's KV must be recomputed or overwritten every cycle, while the Coconut loop in src/coconut.py is append-only), the per-slot gate head, and the multi-slot continuous arms A and B are all new. The only per-step state generator in the repo (src/compose.py) emits a single running value in Z_10, which is M=1; the multi-slot invented-system generators that "already emit the full state after every step" are not here, and I could not find them in ~/Research. Realistic: two to three weeks of one person's time, not one.

Falsifier sharpness: two of four kill conditions carry a number (10x wall-clock, 0.999 per-transition). Conditions 1 and 2 say "fail to beat" and "does not beat" with three seeds and no effect size, which is not a falsifier. Condition 1 is also the one whose outcome is already in the evidence base: continuous carry extrapolates about 1.5x, so A and B collapsing by k=32 is a replication, not a risk. And it is not run at matched supervision, whatever the text says: a continuous carry has no ground-truth state, so A and B must be trained by BPTT through up to eight cycles while C and D are teacher-forced on single transitions. Two variables change at once (carry type and training regime). Condition 2 (gate vs no gate) is a real question, since C's per-slot copy error compounds: at 0.9995 per untouched slot, 29 untouched slots over 256 steps gives 0.986^256 = 0.027 exact-frame, so D could win visibly. But the training signal as written has a flaw that muddies it: the content loss is masked wherever the interpreter says a slot did not change, so the content head is never trained to reproduce a held value, and a single gate false positive on an untouched slot writes an arbitrary token. D can lose to C because of that, which has nothing to do with the hypothesis. Condition 3 depends on which E is chosen: against a full dynamic scratchpad (32 serial decodes per step) 10x is easy; against the compact scratchpad that emits only the three changed slots, the serial-decode ratio is 3-5x and the bar may fail. The experimenter picks.

Condition 4 is the one sharp, risky test, and its likely failure is uninformative. A 20-60M model from scratch reading a 100-300 token prose rulebook for a system invented after training, at 0.999 per transition: the researcher's own 350M fact-free model reached 0.680 on single-step rule application for such systems. On 1dCA the rule is an 8-entry table and 0.999 is plausible; on prose systems it is not, and the failure would say "the model cannot read the rulebook," not "the frame carry does not work." The idea bundles two hypotheses, H1 (discrete in-place carry with exact hold extends serial depth) and H2 (a small model executes in-context prose rules at 0.999 per step), and the breakthrough claim rests on H2, the less likely one. Note also that 0.999^256 = 0.77 and 0.999^1000 = 0.37; passing the stated bar does not deliver "thousands of steps," which needs 0.9999, measurable only with over 10^5 held-out transitions per condition (cheap in teacher-forced batch eval, but not planned).

Would a positive result be a breakthrough? On 1dCA, no: Discrete NAR (discrete carry plus teacher-forced hint transitions gives perfect size generalization), the universal-computer paper (59.5M executes held-out programs perfectly for 7,552 lines), and the Turing-machine snapshot toy all predict arm C and D succeeding on a synchronous 3-neighbor lookup. What is new and testable is the efficiency: one static-shape forward pass per step with bounded context, versus tens of serial decodes. That is a real engineering result with a design principle attached, not a change to anyone's beliefs about depth, unless the held-out prose systems pass at 0.999, in which case it would be a genuine result about in-context execution at small scale.
judges.strongest_objection: The comparison the idea calls decisive (discrete versus continuous carry at "identical per-step supervision") cannot be run at identical supervision, because a continuous carry has no ground-truth state to teacher-force. Arms A and B train by BPTT through the carry; arms C and D train on isolated teacher-forced transitions. Kill condition 1 therefore varies the training regime along with the carry, and its outcome is already known from the evidence base (continuous carry extrapolates about 1.5x). The one numeric, risky test, 0.999 per transition on held-out prose rule systems, will most probably fail because a 20-60M model cannot read a 300-token rulebook to that fidelity (the researcher's 350M got 0.680 on single-step application), a failure that says nothing about whether the frame carry works. The likely ending is the safe arm passing and the interesting arm dying for an unrelated reason, which is a datapoint, not a verdict.
judges.what_survives: The budget, the static-shape latency claim, and a narrower experiment that isolates one variable at a time. Concretely: (1) Add a teacher-forceable continuous arm, feeding back the ground-truth embedding E[v] plus Gaussian noise (or the softmax-expected embedding with straight-through) so discrete versus continuous carry is tested under the same teacher-forced transitions; that is the arm that actually tests "nothing crosses the boundary but the readout." (2) Split H1 from H2. Test the carry on rule systems where per-transition accuracy saturates (in-weights rules, or 1dCA tables in context), so the extrapolation curve to k=256 isolates the carry. Separately, measure in-context rule reading at k=1 on held-out prose systems as a function of rulebook length and model size (20M, 60M, and the 350M checkpoint); this is a single teacher-forced run per size, under $10, and should go first, because if 60M sits below 0.999 the execution-cortex claim is dead before the 30-run sweep is paid for. (3) Apply the content loss on all slots, or on a sample of unchanged ones, so a gate false positive reproduces the held value instead of garbage; otherwise D versus C measures a training-signal bug. (4) Put numbers on conditions 1 and 2: for example, at k=32 and M=32 on held-out rules, C and D exact-frame at or above 0.9 on all three seeds with A and B at or below 0.3; for the gate, D minus C at k=256 at or above 0.05 exact-frame on every seed, plus a direct measurement of C's per-slot copy error, which is the mechanism that would explain any gap. (5) Frame the wall-clock test against the compact scratchpad, not the full one, and report serial decodes per step alongside milliseconds, since the honest value of the idea is a bounded-context executor at one forward pass per step. (6) Set the per-transition bar at 0.9999 with over 10^5 held-out transitions per condition if the claim is thousands of steps; 0.999 supports a few hundred. The hold gate as a literal identity on integers, supervised from the interpreter diff, is the one component with no prior and a clean mechanism, and it survives as the thing worth measuring on its own.

idea.lens: Theoretical computer science: the transformer as a circuit class, serial depth as the resource, the step-to-step interface as the object that decides whether depth is learnable and extrapolable.
idea.name: Snap-Tape Machine: a closed discrete tape rewritten in place by argmax projection, trained only on single-step transitions, with the program held in a frozen prefix
idea.one_sentence: Replace the serial token trace with a fixed-width tape of W discrete cells that a tiny shared block rewrites in parallel every step by hard argmax (no sampling, no continuous state carried between steps), trained purely on one-step (program, tape_t) -> tape_{t+1} pairs from a reference executor with no backprop through steps, so that serial depth becomes an inference-time loop count on a static-shape stepper rather than a property of parameter count or of emitted tokens.
idea.mechanism: Context has two regions. (1) Program prefix P: ordinary tokens (the rule table, axioms, or source code), prefilled once; its K/V are cached and never rewritten for the life of the request. (2) Data tape D_t: W cells (W fixed per request, e.g. 256 to 4096), each an index into a cell alphabet A (for 1dCA, A = {0,1}; for an interpreter, A = variable names, small integers, opcodes, pointer marks, blank; A can be a subset of the LM vocabulary so the final tape is readable as text without ever having been generated serially). Stepper S: a shallow bidirectional transformer block over the tape (4 to 8 layers, d 256 to 512, roughly 10 to 50M params, RoPE or ALiBi), with tape cells attending to all tape cells and to the cached K/V of P. One step is x = Embed(D_t) in R^{W x d}; h = S(x; KV_P); logits = W_out h in R^{W x |A|}; D_{t+1} = argmax over |A| per cell. Nothing else survives the step: h is discarded, there is no residual carry, no KV for the tape is kept, so the tape K/V are recomputed from integers each step (write-many memory implemented by recomputation, while P stays write-once, which matches the stateless-DNC proof in 2603.19272). Halting is a designated HALT cell plus a tape-equality check between fixed chunks of steps, so shapes are static and the whole step is one CUDA graph replay; T steps are T replays. Training signal: per-cell cross-entropy on D_{t+1} given (P, D_t), all W cells in parallel, on trajectories emitted by the researcher's reference implementations and mathgen generators (train and test rule systems disjoint, as in Beyond Memorization). No BPTT through steps, no end-to-end k-step loss, no straight-through estimator, no RL. Optional denoising: corrupt a small fraction of cells in D_t where the executor defines a unique repair, so the stepper's basin of attraction covers near-valid tapes. The knowledge model (the 350M fact-free checkpoint or a MiniCPM5-1B class model) does two jobs only: compile the problem statement into (P, D_0), and read D_final; both are fine-tuned from generator data and checked by the verifier. The formal reason this differs from every latent loop: a step map applied T times is a dynamical system, and reliable T-step computation requires the map to contract onto a discrete attractor set so per-step error is removed. Bengio, Simard and Frasconi (1994) proved that a recurrent map which stores discrete information robustly (contracts) has gradients that vanish exponentially in T. So a latent loop trained by gradient through T steps can be contractive (robust, but unlearnable past a few steps) or gradient-preserving (learnable, but with no closure: its reachable set drifts off the training set, hidden norms grow, and errors compound), and both give a ceiling at small k, which is exactly the observed k~2 for recurrence, +1 for ACT, saturation at step 4 for Ouro, and Saunshi's loops matching the equivalent deep model and stopping. Token CoT escapes because argmax is an infinitely contractive projection whose zero gradient nobody needs, since the per-step target is available, and because the state space is closed under the step: every output is a valid input. The snap-tape keeps both properties and drops the two things tokens do not need: sampling (projection suffices) and seriality (W projections happen at once). Predicted accuracy at depth T is a^T for one-step accuracy a on held-out rules, with no ceiling in T other than a, so a is driven toward 1 by more free one-step data rather than by more parameters.
idea.why_it_could_be_a_breakthrough: Today the belief is that serial depth is the one thing small models cannot buy: the 4B keeps 92 to 101% of the 27B on knowledge and instruction following and only 30 to 69% on depth benchmarks, and the only working cure is serial output tokens (240M of them for the 4B). If the snap-tape works, depth for execution-shaped work becomes an inference-time loop count on a 10 to 50M stepper with static shapes, so a 1B on-device model plus a stepper runs 10^4-step procedures over rules it has never seen in roughly 10^4 block passes over a few thousand cells (seconds on one GPU, CUDA-graphed, no data-dependent shapes), and inherits Universal-Computer-style 60x depth extrapolation in the parallel regime instead of the serial one. The residual gap between small and large models would then be search (finding the procedure), which lives in the compressible knowledge the 4B already retains, and the entire latent-reasoning program (Coconut, looped and recurrent-depth transformers, ACT, fast weights for depth) would be seen as attacking the wrong variable: the interface between steps, not the state or the supervision density, is what caps depth. It would also mean the knowledge model can be quantized and MoE'd freely while the depth lives in a separate tiny module that never needs to be large.
idea.evidence_that_generates_it: Beyond Memorization: k=1 at 0.95 but k=2 at 0.40 and k>=3 below 0.25 with a 4-layer d=128 model, recurrence to k=2 only, ACT +1 with diminishing returns past k~3, depth sweep flat, yet token CoT with stepwise supervision above 90% at k<=4 with the same parameters; and the paper never fed a predicted state back into the one-step model (its O-O variant predicts all k states from mask tokens with no feedback, and it states it avoided autoregressive state chaining on purpose). Universal Computer: 59.5M params, traces capped at 128 lines, perfect at 7,552 lines, every line generated serially. Ouro 1.4B: 41.21, 60.43, 66.71, 67.45 then degradation past trained depth (no closure). Saunshi: 1 layer looped 8x equals the 8-layer model at 73.2 and stops. NLI: removing the discrete program drops 97% to 1%. Stateless DNC proof: causal transformers have write-once memory and no persistent control state. The researcher's own numbers: 0.680 single-step rule application versus 0.000 multi-step composition across thousands of RL steps and six objectives (single-step competence exists, composition through the model's own output does not); textbook in context 0.0283 with well-formedness 0.34 versus retrieved 0.1233 at 0.97 (program tokens leaking into persisted state); GRPO reward_std to 0 four times (end-to-end signal cannot cold-start composition). H200 profiling: data-dependent shapes cannot be graphed, depth must be static per request. Serial output tokens are wall-clock latency (240M tokens for the 4B).
idea.nearest_prior_art: Note on tooling: the exa.sh helper named in the task does not exist in the scratchpad and no Exa key is set, so I used WebSearch and WebFetch (13 searches, 12 paper fetches). Closest hits. (1) "Unlocking Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Transformers via Recursive Latent Space Reasoning" (arXiv 2510.14095): per-token sequence updated each iteration, argmax over a factored vocabulary and re-embed between iterations, per-iteration supervision on values computable within t steps, input-adaptive recurrence and an error-correction mechanism; trained on graphs of up to 32 nodes, near-perfect up to 128 while CoT baselines degrade past about 40. This is the closest mechanism match. Differences: the algorithm is fixed and learned (not read from context; disjoint rule systems are not tested), supervision is dense across iterations with a shared readout rather than pure one-step teacher forcing, and there is no serial-depth study of the k=1 to k=64 kind. (2) "Discrete Neural Algorithmic Reasoning" (arXiv 2402.11628): discrete predefined states plus hint supervision on state transitions, perfect test scores single-task and multitask with provable correctness; GNN, fixed CLRS algorithms, not in-context programs, not a transformer LM. (3) "Training Transformers as a Universal Computer" (arXiv 2604.25166): in-context programs, small-step semantics one line per step, PENCIL erasure, fully serial token generation. (4) "Universal Length Generalization with Turing Programs" (arXiv 2407.03310) and "The Imitation Game: Turing Machine Imitator" (arXiv 2507.13332): serial CoT imitation of TM steps with 2 to 3x length generalization. (5) LOTUS, "Bridging the Gap Between Latent and Explicit Reasoning with Looped Transformers" (arXiv 2606.31779): K latent positions looped R times with cross-entropy on each position's gold CoT token, parity with explicit CoT at 3B and 2.5 to 6.9x lower thought latency; no discretization between loops and a fixed R, no depth extrapolation claim. (6) "Dense Supervision Is Not Enough: The Readout Blind Spot in Looped Language Models" (arXiv 2606.24898): dense per-loop cross-entropy leaves hidden-state scale uncontrolled, norms reach thousands; consistent with the drift half of the thesis, no snap. (7) "What Makes Effective Supervision in Latent Chain-of-Thought" (arXiv 2606.20075): documents gradient attenuation plus representational drift ("dual collapse") and proposes generative reconstruction, explicitly not discretization. (8) "Thinking Deeper, Not Longer" (arXiv 2603.21676): identity-biased recurrence as a gradient highway with final-only supervision, 20+ iterations, continuous; this is the gradient-preserving horn of the tradeoff. (9) Neural GPU (arXiv 1511.08228): parallel learned tape, 20 to 2000 bit generalization on binary multiplication, continuous gates, needed curriculum, gradient noise and relaxed parameter sharing, never trained with one-step targets. (10) "Transformers Can Learn Rules They've Never Seen" (arXiv 2603.17019) and LifeGPT: in-context or autoregressive CA rule application, no discrete-tape depth study on disjoint rules. (11) "A Symbolic Neural CPU" (arXiv 2607.10021): register writeback with discrete semantics, serial, fixed ALU bank. I found no paper that combines programs read from context, a parallel per-cell discrete tape, and one-step-only training with unbounded iteration, and none that states the contraction-versus-gradient impossibility as the reason latent loops cap at k~2 to 4.
idea.what_is_genuinely_new: Four things, stated honestly. (a) The intersection nobody has built: rules or programs read from a frozen context prefix (disjoint train/test rule systems), a parallel per-cell discrete tape rewritten in place by projection, and training that is one-step teacher forcing only, with the loop count a free inference parameter. 2510.14095 and DNAR have the discrete tape for fixed algorithms; Universal Computer and the TM-imitation papers have in-context programs with serial tokens; LOTUS has parallel supervised loops with no snap and fixed R; Beyond Memorization never chained states. (b) The formal claim, which I did not find in the latent-reasoning literature: the k~2 to 4 ceiling is the Bengio-Simard-Frasconi tradeoff applied to shared-weight step maps. A step map cannot be both contractive onto a discrete state set (closure, error correction) and trainable by gradient through many steps, so no density of continuous per-step supervision fixes it (the readout blind spot and dual-collapse findings are the symptoms), and the answer to "supervision or fixed width?" is neither: it is closure of the state space under the step, which tokens get from argmax and which per-cell projection gives without sampling or seriality. Fixed width matters only when the working state exceeds about d usable bits, which is why a single-vector Coconut state is a second, separate bottleneck. (c) The program/data split as an architectural fix, with a specific prediction for the researcher's own anomaly: with the program frozen in the prefix and only the snapped tape persisting, in-context program tokens cannot leak into the working state, so the textbook-in-context well-formedness collapse (0.34) should vanish. (d) A cost model in which the deep part is a 10 to 50M static-shape stepper and the knowledge part only compiles and reads tapes; that split is not present in any of the prior art above.
idea.killing_experiment: 1dCA in the Beyond Memorization setting: rule table in the context prefix, radius-1 (256 rules) and radius-2 (2^32 rules) families, train and test rules disjoint, W = 64 cells, a 4-layer d=256 stepper (~3M params). Train ONLY on one-step pairs (P, D_t) -> D_{t+1}; never show a k>1 trajectory. Four arms, identical data and parameters: A = hard argmax snap between steps, one-step teacher forcing (the proposal); B = same training, but feed the pre-argmax hidden state (or softmax-weighted embedding) back instead of snapping; C = snap, but trained end-to-end through k=4 with straight-through and final-state loss only; D = a continuous shared-weight recurrence trained end-to-end (the Beyond Memorization recurrence baseline). Evaluate exact whole-tape accuracy at k = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 on held-out rules and record the one-step accuracy a. The idea is dead if A at k=16 is at or below 0.25 (the published recurrence ceiling), or if A decays more than 2x faster than a^k by k=16 (the snap confers no closure), or if B matches A at k>=8 (discreteness was irrelevant and supervision was the whole story, which kills the contraction thesis). It survives only if A tracks a^k out to k=64 (with a pushed to about 0.99 by more one-step data, that is 0.85 at k=16 and 0.53 at k=64) while B and D fall below 0.3 by k=4 to 8 and C does not beat A. A second cheap kill: on the researcher's own formal systems, put the textbook in the frozen prefix and run the stepper; if well-formedness of the tape stays near 0.34 rather than rising toward 0.97, prediction (c) is dead. Cost of the CA factorial alone: about two days on one L40S, roughly $60.
idea.cost: About $1,000 of GPU time and 2 to 3 weeks on one L40S or H200 at a time: CA factorial and kill test about $60 (2 days); in-context rule systems from the researcher's generators with a 20 to 50M stepper on a 512-cell tape, including the depth-extrapolation and wall-clock comparison against serial token traces, about $400; compiling from the 350M fact-free checkpoint to (P, D_0) and reading D_final back with the verifier, about $500. Data is free (procedural generators with reference implementations). Well under the $2,000 cap and the $4,700 budget.

judges.lens: NOVELTY (adversarial prior-art search: 26 Exa queries plus primary-source reads of arXiv 2510.14095, 2412.01417, 2202.05826, 2508.16745 and the anadim/subleq-transformer repository)
judges.verdict: The mechanism exists, twice, at exactly the scale proposed. (1) arXiv 2510.14095 (Altabaa, Chen, Lafferty, Yang, Yale, Oct 2025) is not merely "closest": its Appendix B states that the argmax-and-re-embed discrete bottleneck "enables us to train the model with a type of teacher-forcing across recurrent iterations. That is, we can teacher-force the inputs z_i^(t) at each iteration t." Argmax has no gradient, so this is one-step training on discrete states with no BPTT through steps, per token in parallel, with the program instance (the computational graph) read from the input, random corruption of the discrete state during training for error correction (the proposal's "optional denoising"), iteration count scaled at inference from 32-node training to 128-node test, and an explicit ablation "Continuous Latent Space Supervision" (per-step supervised, no snap) versus "Discrete Latent Space Supervision" in which discrete wins. That is arm A versus arm B of the killing experiment, already run. The generator's claim that the algorithm is "not read from context" is wrong in the same sense it would be wrong for 1dCA: the fixed algorithm is "evaluate the graph" there and "apply the rule table" here; the instance is in context in both. (2) anadim/subleq-transformer, round 2 (Papailiopoulos, GitHub, March 2026, written up at dimitrisp.substack.com "Can You Train a Computer?"): a 6-layer bidirectional transformer, d=256, 4.88M params, state = 1 PC cell plus 32 discrete memory cells, trained only on single-step SUBLEQ transitions with per-cell weighted cross-entropy, argmax per cell, looped at inference. 100% single-step on held out states; programs never seen as full executions run correctly: Fibonacci 47 steps 100%, multiply 141/141, division 91 steps 93.8%, isqrt 61 steps 95%. The program lives in the tape, so this is a learned universal-ISA executor with a parallel discrete tape, one-step supervision, and depth as a loop count, on a laptop in 4 hours. A 2023 precursor (JackCai1206/Training-Looped-Transformers, with Rajput) attempted the same. (3) arXiv 2412.01417 (Burtsev) already ran the RO-S variant of the researcher's own benchmark: rule table given in context plus orbit, predict next state, held-out rules, then autoregressive rollouts of 2 to 4 steps that beat look-ahead prediction. (4) arXiv 2110.04169 (Ruiz, Ainslie, Ontanon): one-step training, discrete outputs fed back as inputs until an end-of-iteration token, 100% on Cartesian products longer than training. (5) DNAR arXiv 2402.11628 and Neural Execution Engines (NeurIPS 2020) supply the discrete-state-plus-transition-supervision pattern in GNN and transformer form. What is left unoccupied is a benchmark cell (disjoint-rule 1dCA, rule in a frozen prefix, k to 64 with an a^k fit) and an engineering detail (frozen KV prefix for the program). Those are a measurement, not an architecture.
judges.strongest_objection: The theoretical spine, the claim that a shared-weight step map cannot be both contractive onto a discrete attractor set and trainable by gradient, so continuous loops are capped at k~2 to 4 and only argmax escapes, is contradicted by arXiv 2202.05826 (Bansal, Schwarzschild et al., NeurIPS 2022): a fully continuous recurrent network trained with at most 30 iterations, using a progressive loss that detaches the state after a random n iterations and backpropagates through only k more (their words: an analog of truncated BPTT with random start and end), solves 801x801 mazes with 20,000 iterations, a 600x depth extrapolation with no discretization anywhere. arXiv 2507.02782 (Buitrago Ruiz and Gu) gives the same diagnosis the proposal gives (the "unexplored states hypothesis": drift comes from training on a subset of reachable states) and fixes it continuously by initializing training states from other trajectories. So the variable that matters is training the step map from on-distribution reachable states with short-horizon gradients; argmax is one way to guarantee that and not the only one. The proposed four-arm factorial has no continuous detached-and-recall arm, so it cannot distinguish "discreteness is the cause" from "reachable-state coverage is the cause", and the one ablation it does contain (snap versus no snap under per-step supervision) is already published in 2510.14095. Bengio, Simard and Frasconi 1994 is being cited for a claim their theorem does not make.
judges.what_survives: Three things, none of them the architecture. (1) The empty cell in the matrix is in-context interpretation of unseen rule systems over a parallel discrete tape: 2510.14095 has a fixed set of modular operations, the SUBLEQ executor has a fixed ISA, and 2412.01417 chains only 2 to 4 steps serially. Nobody has shown a parallel per-cell stepper reading a rule table it has never seen from a prefix and iterating it 64 steps. The $60 CA factorial answers that, provided a fifth arm is added: Bansal-style continuous recurrence with recall and detached truncated training. If that arm matches the snap arm, the interesting result is that closure comes from state coverage, not discreteness, which is publishable and reframes the whole latent-reasoning debate; if it fails where the snap succeeds, the contraction thesis gains its first real evidence. Either outcome is a finding; the current design only replicates. (2) The frozen program prefix with only the snapped tape persisting is a specific, unclaimed prediction about the researcher's own anomaly (well-formedness 0.34 with the textbook in context versus 0.97 retrieved). Testing whether the split eliminates the collapse costs almost nothing and is not in any prior work. (3) The depth-extrapolation ratio on a parallel tape is unmeasured: the SUBLEQ executor trained on 1 to 8 instruction steps and ran 91, roughly 10x; Universal Computer got 60x serially. Whether a parallel tape reaches 60x with rules read from context, and at what one-step accuracy a, is a number nobody has. Drop the breakthrough framing, drop the Bengio 1994 argument, keep the factorial with the extra arm and the researcher's formal systems as the test bed.

judges.verdict:
Number-by-number check, with two claims in the idea verified against the primary papers.

What checks out. (1) Beyond Memorization: the metric is exact match of the whole state; models were trained separately per k; the O-O variant predicts all k states from mask tokens and the paper states predicted states are not fed back. The idea's reading of the paper is correct: nobody chained the k=1 model on its own output. Baseline 0.95/0.40/<0.25/<0.25, ARMT ~0.95/0.20, ACT 0.95/0.55/0.25/0.20, CoT >0.90 through k=4 are all as the evidence base states, and the idea uses them correctly. (2) Ouro 41.21/60.43/66.71/67.45 then degrading past trained depth, Saunshi 1x8 = 8-layer at 73.2 and stopping, and the 32-operand addition result being log-depth parallel are all consistent with the contraction-versus-gradient reading; none contradicts it, though none uniquely supports it either. (3) Universal Computer (59.5M, 128-line cap, perfect at 7,552 lines) is the strongest support: one-step supervision plus a closed discrete state extrapolating 60x in step count. (4) The stateless-DNC proof, the NTM/DNC failure modes, and the H200 profiling (static shapes, 34.8% graphed) are all respected by the design; the tape is write-many by recomputation, P is write-once, no soft addressing survives a step, every step is one graph replay. Tensor shapes, the per-cell cross-entropy target, the absence of BPTT, and halting via HALT cell plus equality check are all coherent. (5) 2510.14095, verified: it discretizes per-token state by argmax over factored vocabularies, re-embeds, supervises every iteration, trains on N<=32 and is near-perfect at N=128 while CoT degrades past ~40, and its ablation without discretization drifts. Since argmax passes no gradient, that paper is effectively already the idea's arm A versus arm B for a fixed algorithm, and it came out the way the idea predicts. This supports feasibility and means the CA factorial is largely confirmatory rather than a kill test.

Where the numbers do not point where the generator says. (a) The a^T claim. The only verified one-step exact-match number on held-out in-context rules is 0.95 (4-layer, d=128). At a=0.95, a^16=0.44 and a^64=0.037; the survival criterion needs a=0.99. Nothing in the evidence base shows one-step exact match on disjoint rules rising with more data; the CoT >0.90 at k=4 implies an effective per-step rate of at least 0.974, but that came with serial per-cell generation and 4x the supervised transitions, so it does not isolate data volume. Worse, a is a whole-tape quantity: a = p^W for per-cell reliability p. a=0.99 at W=64 needs p=0.99984; at W=512 it needs p=0.99998; the breakthrough claim (10^4 steps over a few thousand cells) needs a per-cell error near 10^-8 on rules never seen in training. UC's 7,552 perfect lines (roughly 10^5 tokens, so per-token error below 10^-5) is the best verified figure and it is three orders of magnitude short, in the serial regime with unbounded within-step depth. The idea says "no ceiling in T other than a" and never confronts the W factor. (b) Prediction (c) is inconsistent with the anomaly it claims to explain. A standard autoregressive LM already has a discrete, closed state between tokens (every emitted token is a hard projection; the residual stream is recomputed from tokens each pass), and the in-context textbook still drove well-formedness to 0.34 versus 0.97 retrieved. Whatever caused that happens inside a single forward pass with P in context, which the stepper also has at every step. The snap removes nothing there; if the second kill test passes it will be because the cell alphabet A excludes program tokens by construction, which says nothing about the thesis. (c) The 4B/27B depth gap (LiveCodeBench 69, TIR-Bench 65, OSWorld 63, OJBench 60, BabyVision 36, ZEROBench 30) is search, tool use, and perception, not execution of a given procedure. The idea half-admits this ("residual gap would be search") but still frames those numbers as what it fixes. The only execution-shaped numbers in the base are the 1dCA table and the researcher's 0.000 on multi-step composition, and those are the honest target. (d) The researcher's 0.680 single-step figure is cited as "single-step competence exists"; at a=0.68, a^4=0.21. It was an RL-tuned 350M LM, not a dedicated stepper, so it is not a kill, but it is a warning the idea reads generously. (e) The 240M-token latency figure is for an aggregate reasoning index, not for execution traces; it motivates nothing specific about this design.

Mechanism gap the 1dCA test cannot see. Per-cell independent argmax has no joint-consistency guarantee. For a rule that fires at one position (leftmost match, pointer moves, the researcher's rewriting systems), cell i may decide "rule 3 at position 7" while cell j decides "rule 5 at position 2"; per-cell CE never penalizes the joint inconsistency, and serial CoT gets this for free by conditioning later cells on earlier ones. 1dCA is local, so arm A will not expose this. The framework can absorb it with mark-then-apply micro-steps at 2x T, but the idea does not say so and its a^T model does not account for it.
judges.strongest_objection: The headline "no ceiling in T other than a" hides that a is p^W, and the single verified one-step exact-match number on held-out in-context rules is 0.95, which gives 0.44 at k=16 and 0.04 at k=64 for W=64. To reach the claimed regime (10^4 steps, thousands of cells, unseen rules) the stepper needs a per-cell error near 10^-8; the best verified reliability anywhere in the evidence base is UC's roughly 10^-5 per token, achieved serially with unbounded within-step depth. No number in the base shows one-step exact match on disjoint rules moving from 0.95 toward 0.99 with data, and the whole proposal rests on that unmeasured slope.
judges.what_survives: The core is consistent with every number and is worth the $60: an argmax-snapped parallel tape, rules in a frozen prefix, pure one-step teacher forcing, exact-match at k=1..64 on disjoint 1dCA rules, with a recorded per-step a. Reframe it honestly: 2510.14095 already shows discrete-vs-continuous drift for a fixed algorithm, so arms A and B are a replication; the open questions are (1) whether one-step exact match on held-out in-context rules climbs past 0.95 with free data and how per-cell error scales with W (measure p directly, not just a), (2) joint consistency of independent per-cell projections on non-local rules, tested on the researcher's own rewriting systems with mark-then-apply micro-steps as the fallback, and (3) wall-clock versus a UC-style serial trace at matched accuracy. Drop prediction (c), the 4B/27B depth-benchmark framing, and the 10^4-step scale claim until p is measured; the contraction-versus-gradient reading of the k~2 to 4 ceiling is a reasonable and unrefuted interpretation, but it is an interpretation, not a prediction the evidence base can yet distinguish from "supervision plus on-distribution feedback."

judges.lens: Testability: can the killing experiment be run for under $2,000 on one GPU by one person, is the falsifier a specific number, and would a positive result be a breakthrough or a datapoint.
judges.verdict: Cheap, nominally sharp, not decisive. Cost is not in question: a 3M-parameter stepper on 64-cell tapes with radius-1 and radius-2 rule tables in a prefix of 8 to 64 tokens trains in minutes to an hour per arm on an L40S, and the radius-1 case would run overnight on the researcher's M2 Pro. The repo has no CA generator (src/ holds coconut.py, pipeline.py, compose.py, tasks.py and the ProsQA/HotpotQA plumbing), but writing one is a few dozen lines of numpy, and the Coconut codebase is largely irrelevant since the stepper is a fresh bidirectional block with no LM. Call it $20 to $60 and two or three days of work, well under the cap. The problem is what the run can tell you. Three defects. First, 1dCA is the one task where the proposal's central mechanism is trivially satisfied: every binary string is a valid tape, so closure of the state space under the step holds for any model that emits bits, and the step itself is per-cell local with no within-step serial structure, so the parallel tape is the natural model class rather than a discovery. Arm A succeeding is close to guaranteed given Beyond Memorization's 0.95 at k=1 and 2603.17019's in-context CA rule application, and success there says nothing about interpreter-shaped states where most strings are invalid and a step has internal dependencies, which is where the breakthrough claim lives. Second, the 2x2 that would answer the stated question (discrete vs continuous carry crossed with dense vs final-only supervision) is missing the one cell that matters. A is (discrete, dense), C is (discrete, final), D is (continuous, final). The cell (continuous, dense), a carry of h_t trained on its own chained states with per-step cross-entropy, is absent. Arm B as written trains on one-hot embeddings and tests on softmax embeddings, so it fails from distribution shift if the softmax is soft and matches A if the softmax is sharp, and neither outcome bears on the contraction thesis. The proposal's third kill criterion (B matches A at k>=8 kills the thesis) would fire precisely when a is high, because a confident softmax is already a near-projection. Third, the numeric thresholds are not anchored to the experiment's own error model. The 0.25 floor is borrowed from a different architecture in a different paper, and the a^k prediction assumes independent per-step, per-tape errors, whereas stepper errors on a held-out rule are systematic (a misread rule entry fails every time that neighborhood appears), and CA dynamics either absorb perturbations (class 1 and 2 rules) or spread them at one cell per step (class 3 and 4), so the "decays more than 2x faster than a^k" clause can be crossed or not by the rule mix rather than by anything about the snap. The second cheap kill, well-formedness on the researcher's own formal systems with the textbook frozen in the prefix (0.34 should move toward 0.97), is the sharpest item on the list and does not depend on the CA run. A positive CA result is a datapoint that Neural CA and in-context rule papers already imply; a negative one would be surprising and worth publishing but is unlikely.
judges.strongest_objection: The factorial cannot separate supervision from discreteness because it omits the continuous-carry, dense-supervision arm trained on its own chained states, and substitutes an arm (B) whose behavior is governed by softmax temperature rather than by the property under test. The proposal's own framing says the open question is whether supervision is the whole story; the experiment as designed reproduces the confound it set out to remove, on a task (1dCA) where closure and per-cell locality hold for free, so arm A wins for reasons that do not transfer to structured tapes.
judges.what_survives: The run is cheap enough that it should happen before further argument, but redesigned: add the (continuous carry, dense per-step supervision, trained on its own states, truncated BPTT) arm, sweep softmax temperature in B so the discrete-to-continuous transition is a curve rather than a single point, report per-rule accuracy trajectories stratified by Wolfram class instead of a pooled a^k fit, and set the kill threshold against the experiment's own arm D rather than a number from another paper. The well-formedness prediction on the researcher's invented formal systems (frozen textbook prefix, snapped tape, expect 0.34 to rise toward 0.97) is a specific, system-bound falsifier that stands on its own and costs almost nothing given the existing generators and verifier. The static-shape, CUDA-graphable stepper as an engineering target survives independent of the contraction argument: the H200 profiling already showed data-dependent shapes cannot be graphed, and a fixed-width tape with a fixed loop count is a shape that can. What does not survive is the claim that a CA result would test the breakthrough; the decisive experiment is the 512-cell interpreter tape over invented rule systems, where a state space that is mostly invalid strings makes closure non-trivial and within-step dependencies make per-cell parallelism a real constraint.

idea.lens: Hardware-first design: design backwards from what an H100 runs at full occupancy with static, graphable shapes (a batched stencil over on-chip data), and from what a pbit array does natively (a local discrete update with compiled couplings). The constraint is the design.
idea.name: Stencil Tape: compile once, sweep many
idea.one_sentence: Serial depth cannot be parallelized away for P-complete rule composition, so make each serial step a stencil sweep over a discrete on-chip tape whose update rule is compiled per problem into a few kilobytes of weights; the language model is a compiler and a decoder, never the executor.
idea.mechanism: State: an int8 tape T_t of shape [B, W] (B problems in the batch, W cells, V symbols; V=2 for 1dCA, about 64 for the researcher's invented formal systems) plus one HALT flag per tape. Executor: a per-cell MLP f applied to a radius-r window of one-hot cells (input (2r+1)*V, hidden 128 to 256, output V logits), with an optional single global-read head (one attention over the W cells at d=32) so pointer-style moves do not cost O(W) sweeps. Base weights theta (about 100 KB) are shared across problems. Compiler C_phi (a small transformer for the 1dCA benchmark; the 350M fact-free checkpoint with a LoRA-emitting head for formal systems) reads the program description exactly once (the 10-state orbit in the 1dCA benchmark, where the rule must be induced; the textbook text for formal systems) and emits a per-problem low-rank delta on the executor's first layer plus a bias vector, a few KB per problem. One step: logits = f_{theta + delta_b}(window(T_t)); T_{t+1} = argmax(logits); writes are masked on halted tapes. N sweeps run for every tape in the batch (static N, CUDA-graphable), and halting is a tape symbol rather than a control-flow branch, which matches the profiling finding that depth must be static per request. Training signal: teacher-forced per-cell cross-entropy at every step against the reference trace (gold T*_t in, T*_{t+1} as target). For W=32 and N=64 that is 2048 supervised targets per problem, dense from step one, so there is no reward_std collapse and no cold start. Gradients reach the compiler through delta_b from every cell at every step, but the discrete rollout itself is never in the gradient path (Kortical's hard-unrolled STE lost to soft unrolling, 65.5% vs 96.7%, precisely when the rollout had to carry rule-inference gradient). Scheduled sampling at p=0.1 feeds the executor its own argmax so it learns to recover from its own errors. Inference: executor weights, per-problem deltas, and the tapes (B*W bytes) all fit in shared memory; one sweep at B=1024, W=128, h=256, V=64 is about 10 GFLOP, roughly 20 to 50 microseconds on an H100, so 10^4 serial steps for 1024 problems takes under a second. The LM runs once to compile and once to read the final tape.
idea.why_it_could_be_a_breakthrough: If it works, a 355M-parameter system executes 10^4-step exact serial reasoning on rules it has never seen, in under a second per batch, on one GPU. Reasoning depth would be decoupled from both parameter count and token throughput. Today depth is the one capability that does not compress (Qwen3.5-4B keeps 92 to 101% of the 27B on MMLU-Pro, IFEval, TAU2 but only 30 to 69% on LiveCodeBench, OSWorld, ZEROBench) and small reasoners pay for depth in serial output tokens (about 240M for the 4B at AA Index 20 versus 38M for Gemma 4 31B at index 30). If depth runs in the right substrate at microseconds per step, a 1B-class device model could out-execute a 27B on formal, verifiable, deep tasks, and the depth gap would be reattributed from model size to execution substrate. It would also give the token/latent tension a mechanism rather than a shrug: token execution works because the state is re-discretized every step, every step is supervised, and the program lives in a medium that does not drift; latent recurrence gives up all three. It fills the measured gap that no fast-weight paper has tested serial depth, and because a per-cell discrete update with compiled couplings is a Boltzmann-machine cell, the design ports to Extropic-style pbit hardware instead of dying with von Neumann GPUs.
idea.evidence_that_generates_it: Beyond Memorization: the same 4-layer d=128 GPT-NeoX scores 0.95 at k=1, 0.40 at k=2, below 0.25 at k=3 and 4 "regardless of depth"; ARMT reaches k=2; ACT adds about one step; yet token CoT with stepwise targets exceeds 90% at k<=4. The failing and succeeding arms differ only in per-step discretization and per-step supervision, not in parameters. The Universal Computer result (59.5M params, perfect at 7,552 trace lines, 60x extrapolation, interpreter in weights, program in context) shows program-in-weights executors extrapolate while latent loops do not (Ouro 41.21 to 67.45 then degrades past trained depth; Saunshi's 1-layer x8 loop matches an 8-layer model at 73.2 and stops; 12 loops solve 32-operand addition only because addition is log-depth). The researcher's own 350M model: 0.9474 on facts, 0.680 on single-step rule application, 0.000 on multi-step composition across thousands of RL steps under six objectives; textbook in context 0.0283 with well-formedness collapsing to 0.34 versus retrieved 0.1233 at 0.97. Program tokens in the residual stream compete with computation and win, so the program has to leave the stream. The Stateless DNC proof says transformers lack read-modify-write and persistent control state; the tape is exactly that, and argmax per step removes the soft addressing whose chained reads degrade exponentially (1904.10278). Hardware: recurrence at 10% utilization eager and 34.8% CUDA-graphed with data-dependent shapes ungraphable; megakernels move vLLM from 39% to 62% of speed-of-light, so the overhead is software; Persistent RNNs got 30x at batch 4 by stashing weights on chip; TTT layers sat below 5% FLOPs utilization because of small online minibatches, which a single compile pass avoids. FrogNano shows synthetic tasks calibrated to the learnability frontier beat real data (1500 synthetic 61.5 vs 1500 real 53.4), and the researcher's generators with reference implementations provide dense trace supervision at any depth.
idea.nearest_prior_art: Searched 14 exa queries and fetched 7 papers. Closest items: (1) Neural GPU (Kaiser & Sutskever 2015, arXiv 1511.08228) and Extensions and Limitations (Price, Zaremba, Sutskever 2016, arXiv 1611.00736): a convolutional GRU grid executor that learned binary and decimal arithmetic and generalized to long inputs, but continuous state, rule fixed in weights, final-output loss, fragile. (2) Discrete Neural Algorithmic Reasoning (Rodionov & Prokhorenkova 2024, arXiv 2402.11628): argmax state bottleneck, hard attention, teacher forcing on state transitions, perfect OOD on SALSA-CLRS up to 1600 nodes where PGN gets 84.5% on Dijkstra.
