This is the strongest prior for the discrete-state component; the algorithm is fixed in weights, there is no per-problem compile, no serial-depth benchmark on unseen rules, and no hardware angle. (3) Robinson 2020 (arXiv 2003.08494): activation binning to stop drift in algorithmic RNNs. (4) Persistent RNNs (Diamos et al., ICML 2016): recurrent weights in the register file, 2.8 TFLOP/s and 30x over GEMM at batch 4 on TitanX; NVIDIA cuda-samples issue #418 (May 2026) proposes the same for microGPT. (5) Text-to-LoRA (Sakana, ICML 2025, arXiv 2506.06105), HINT (ACL 2023), TeNet (arXiv 2601.15912): a hypernetwork compiles a description into adapter or policy weights used once; none target serial depth. (6) NCA Manifold (arXiv 2006.12155) and HyperNCA (arXiv 2204.11674): hypernetwork-generated CA kernels for images and RL policies. (7) Burtsev 2024 (arXiv 2412.01417) and Beyond Memorization (ACL Findings 2026): the benchmark itself, W=20, r=2, evaluated only to k=4. (8) Kortical 2026 (arXiv 2603.17019): 2-layer transformer, 4-step unroll on width-101 CA, soft unrolling 96.7% vs hard 65.5% for inferring a held-out rule entry. (9) LOTUS (Fan, Svete, Lee 2026, arXiv 2606.31779): looped padded transformer, K=6 blocks, R=6 iterations, per-step CE on gold CoT tokens, continuous latents between iterations, full 3B backbone inside the loop, 70.0 vs 71.5 on GSM8K. (10) TRM (arXiv 2510.04871): 7M recursive net, 45% on ARC-AGI-1, continuous latent, task fixed. (11) Transformer VM (Percepta 2026) and Tracr: analytic compilation of programs into transformer weights, not learned, not per problem. Nothing found that compiles an inferred rule into a discrete-state executor's weights per problem, tests serial depth on disjoint rules past k=4, or sizes the executor to shared memory as a design constraint.
idea.what_is_genuinely_new: Four things. First, the inversion of NLI: NLI needs a discrete program and a continuous executor (removing the discrete program drops 97% to 1%); here the program is continuous (per-problem weights) and the state is discrete. This makes "where the program lives" the experimental variable and tests compile-into-weights against attend-over-context on the serial-depth benchmark, which nobody has done. Second, a per-problem compiled executor trained with per-step discrete supervision where the compiler is in the gradient path and the rollout is not, a split that Kortical's numbers argue for and no prior executor uses. Third, the hardware contract: a reasoning step is a stencil sweep sized to shared memory and the LM is touched twice per problem, so serial-depth wall-clock is independent of LM size; Persistent RNNs had the trick but no reasoning claim, DNAR had the discreteness but no hardware claim. Fourth, the prediction itself: above 90% exact match at k>=32 on held-out rules with a 1 to 5M executor, where the literature stops at k=4 and every latent method sits below 0.25 at k=3.
idea.killing_experiment: Replicate 1dCA-Reasoning (W=20 to 64, r=2, disjoint train and test rules, 10-state orbit input, rule induced not given) and extend evaluation to k in {1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128}. Five arms on identical data with a matched executor budget of about 2M params, 3 seeds each: A, token CoT baseline (4-layer GPT-NeoX d=128, stepwise targets) run past k=4 to find where it dies; B, Stencil Tape (compile plus discrete state plus per-step CE); C, attend instead of compile (rule enters through cross-attention from each cell to the orbit at every step); D, no discretization (continuous state between steps, same supervision); E, no per-step supervision (final-state loss, STE through the rollout). Kill: B below 0.5 exact match at k=8 on held-out rules, or per-cell per-step error above 1e-3 on held-out rules, which compounds to failure near k=100 and kills the depth claim. Demotion: if C matches B at every k within confidence intervals, compile-to-weights adds nothing and the idea collapses to DNAR-style discrete execution; the hardware claim would survive, the architectural claim would not. Second gate: measure wall-clock per sweep at B=1024 under CUDA graphs; if a sweep is not under 200 microseconds before any kernel work, the hardware thesis is wrong. Third stage only if B survives: the 350M fact-free checkpoint as compiler emitting LoRAs from the invented-system textbooks, executor on a 128-cell tape with the global-read head, trace supervision from the reference implementations, measured on the multi-step composition task where the researcher currently scores 0.000.
idea.cost: 1dCA stage: 5 arms x 3 seeds x about 3 L40S-hours, plus depth sweeps, roughly 100 GPU-hours, $150 to $300. Formal-systems stage with the 350M compiler: 50 to 100 H200-hours, $200 to $400. Triton persistent-kernel work for the microsecond claim: about 20 GPU-hours. Total $500 to $800 and two to three weeks of one-GPU time, under the $2,000 cap with room for a second round.

judges.verdict:
The exact artifact (LM-compiled per-problem low-rank delta on a discrete-state stencil executor, per-step CE, scored on serial depth over held-out rules, sized to shared memory) does not exist as one paper. Every one of the four "genuinely new" claims, however, is already occupied by a paper the generator missed, and the pieces are close enough that the proposal reads as a recombination rather than an architectural break.

Claim 1, "program in weights, state discrete, compile-vs-attend as the experimental variable": Program-as-Weights (arXiv 2607.02512, July 2026) is a 4B compiler that reads a spec once and emits a LoRA for a frozen 0.6B interpreter, with the same "invoke the foundation model once per function definition" framing; Compile by Training (arXiv 2609.04199) is its follow-up. Learning to Compile Programs to Neural Networks (Weber et al., ICML 2024, arXiv 2407.15078) is a hypernetwork from program text to executor weights. CoDA (Kirchmeyer et al., ICML 2022, arXiv 2202.01889) is literally a per-environment low-rank weight delta produced by a hypernetwork from a context vector, used to roll out dynamics on unseen systems. The compile-vs-attend question itself is the subject of Kobayashi et al. 2024 (arXiv 2407.12275), who found in-context transformers fail to generalize compositionally until a bottleneck separates task inference from execution, of Schug et al. 2023 (arXiv 2312.15001) and Attention as a Hypernetwork (arXiv 2406.05816), and, for program induction specifically, of Devlin et al. 2017 (arXiv 1710.04157), who compared portfolio-adapted weights against k-shot context on Karel.

Claim 2, "per-step discrete supervision, compiler in the gradient path, rollout not": Altabaa et al. 2025 (arXiv 2510.14095) build a recurrent transformer with argmax re-embedding every iteration, per-step algorithmic supervision, and random state corruption during training so the model learns to self-correct, and report near-perfect OOD on computational graphs four times larger than training (N<=32 to N=128) with iterations scaling with graph depth. That is the Stencil Tape training recipe minus the hypernetwork, already shown to extend depth. "Rollout not in the gradient path" is teacher forcing, standard in NAR since CLRS hints and DNAR.

Claim 3, the hardware contract: Roska and Chua's CNN Universal Machine (IEEE TCAS-II 1993, CNNUC3 64x64 chip) is a stored-program analog stencil array whose local templates are loaded per algorithm and iterated on-chip, which is the pbit/stencil story from 33 years ago. Fully fused MLPs with weights in shared memory are tiny-cuda-nn (Muller 2021). Running many stencil time steps on-chip is deep temporal blocking (AN5D 2020; arXiv 2306.03336). Loom (arXiv 2604.08816) is a looped transformer with fixed per-step cost where the program lives in the state tensor. DiffLogic CA (arXiv 2506.04912) already gives a discrete-state learned local rule that runs as a plain circuit at inference and learns Game of Life exactly.

Claim 4, the depth prediction: Deep Thinking (arXiv 2106.04537; arXiv 2202.05826) showed a recurrent conv stencil extrapolating to far more iterations than trained on mazes and prefix sums, with fixed rules and continuous state. AutomataGPT (arXiv 2506.17333) does one-step forecasting and rule reconstruction on unseen 2D CA rules. Elser 2020 (arXiv 2012.02179) reconstructs a 1D CA rule exactly from a single orbit by constraint projection, no network needed.

Also, the evidence base's line that nobody has measured fast weights on serial depth is overstated: Irie et al. NeurIPS 2021 (arXiv 2106.06295) evaluated recurrent fast weight programmers on code execution and sequential ListOps. Not 1dCA, but not nobody.
judges.strongest_objection: For every task the researcher owns, the dominating compile target is symbolic, not a weight delta. A radius-2 binary CA rule is a 32-entry table; the invented formal systems come with reference implementations. An LM that emits the table or the code, plus a fixed exact interpreter (the Universal Computer result at 59.5M params is perfect at 7,552 trace lines with the program in context; PAL-style code execution is perfect at any depth), wins at every k with zero per-cell error, so the learned executor with compiled soft weights is a strictly lossier version of a baseline that already exists. Elser 2020 shows the rule-inference step for 1dCA is a solved constraint problem. The proposal names no task where the rule is inexpressible enough that a neural executor is needed, so arms B and C of the killing experiment measure a distinction the exact-interpreter baseline makes moot. Strip that away and what remains is DNAR/Altabaa discrete execution plus a CoDA/PAW hypernetwork delta applied to the Burtsev benchmark, which is a measurement paper, the thing the researcher said they do not want.
judges.what_survives: One unfilled experiment: on Beyond Memorization's disjoint-rule 1dCA, a matched contrast between a compiled per-problem delta (arm B) and cross-attention to the orbit (arm C), both with an argmax tape and per-step CE, evaluated at k from 8 to 128. Kobayashi 2024 predicts B beats C; Altabaa 2025 predicts C with a discrete bottleneck may already clear the depth wall. Nobody has run that pair on a serial-depth benchmark with held-out rules, and the answer would say something about the token-vs-latent tension. Do it with the exact-interpreter baseline as a ceiling, cite PAW and CoDA as the compile-side prior art, and drop the pbit and shared-memory framing, which CNN-UM and temporal blocking already own. The third stage (350M compiler emitting LoRAs for a discrete executor on the invented formal systems, where the researcher scores 0.000) is the only stage without a direct predecessor, and it only matters if a task is chosen where the reference implementation cannot simply be the executor.

judges.verdict:
Number-by-number check. Citations that match the base: Qwen3.5-4B retention (92-101 vs 30-69), Beyond Memorization (0.95/0.40/<0.25, ARMT k=2, ACT +1, token CoT >90% at k<=4), Ouro 41.21 to 67.45, Saunshi 73.2 and 12 loops on log-depth addition, the researcher's 0.9474/0.680/0.000 and 0.0283@0.34 vs 0.1233@0.97, FrogNano 61.5 vs 53.4, H200 10%/34.8% with static depth, megakernels 39 to 62, TTT under 5%. Out-of-base citations verified against primary sources: Kortical 96.7/65.5/63.1 (2603.17019), DNAR argmax state plus hard attention plus teacher forcing with exact generalization to 1600 nodes (2402.11628), Persistent RNNs 2.8 TFLOP/s at batch 4 and 30x over 0.099 TFLOP/s GEMM, Universal Computer 59.5M/7,552 lines/100%. No number is fabricated.

Where the evidence points the other way. (1) Universal Computer is misread. The idea writes "interpreter in weights, program in context" and then concludes it "shows program-in-weights executors extrapolate." The procedure definitions sit in the prompt, the model executes retrieval steps that look them up, and PENCIL erasure bounds the context. The strongest deep-execution result in the base is arm C (attend), not arm B (compile). (2) NLI without test-time search scores 0.00/0.00/0.17 OOD and reaches 0.99/1.00/0.91 only with 100 gradient steps from 1024 restarts. Single-pass amortized program inference failed OOD in the one place it was measured; the Stencil Tape compiler reads the description exactly once and is scored on held-out rules by construction. The idea cites NLI's 97 to 1 and omits this number. (3) The 350M checkpoint scores 0.0283 with the textbook in context, well-formedness 0.34. Stage 3 proposes that same checkpoint reading that same textbook once and emitting the whole rule set as a LoRA, a strictly harder task than applying one rule. Dense trace CE improves the gradient but the compiler head still reads the residual stream that collapsed. (4) Kortical is cited backwards. Its finding is that rule inference from indirect signal requires gradient through the multi-step rollout (soft 96.7, no unrolling 63.1 equals output bias, hard 65.5). The idea uses it to justify removing the rollout from the gradient path; that is only safe because every cell at every step is directly supervised, which makes the citation irrelevant rather than supportive. Kortical also needed 220 epochs of per-rule gradient descent to recover one hidden XOR entry (47/60 runs); the compiler must do the equivalent in one amortized forward pass per unseen rule.

Mechanism faults. (a) Scheduled sampling at p=0.1 against gold targets: for a deterministic rule, feeding the executor its own wrong tape and asking for the gold next tape trains it to output what gold would be regardless of input, i.e. to violate the rule. Targets must be the reference implementation re-run on the corrupted tape. (b) Error compounding: at the idea's own 1e-3 per-cell-per-step gate with W=128, the expected first error is near step 8; the 10^4-step headline needs about 1e-7. In practice error is per-problem (table right or wrong), so the headline reduces to compile accuracy on unseen rules, which is point 2. (c) For 1dCA at r=2, V=2 the program is a 32-bit truth table and a CA with the right table is exact forever; the 1dCA stage measures induction accuracy, not depth, so B passing at k=128 carries little information about the executor. (d) Pbit port: the Z1 Gibbs-samples an Ising model with pairwise couplings; a 5-input boolean rule is generally not linearly separable, so it needs hidden pbits and several sweeps per step, and sampling reintroduces the per-cell noise the argmax thesis exists to remove. (e) FLOPs: V=64, W=128, B=1024, h=256 is about 26 GFLOP as dense one-hot matmul, about 5 GFLOP as a gather; 20 us at 26 GFLOP exceeds H100 peak, so the 20 to 50 us figure holds only under the gather formulation. The 200 us gate is sound.

Net: no verified number kills the executor; DNAR and Universal Computer support discrete state plus per-step supervision. Several verified numbers predict the compile-to-weights half, which is the entire claimed novelty, is either unnecessary (Universal Computer) or will fail OOD (NLI, the 0.0283). The idea's own demotion clause is where the evidence points, and the researcher said a recombination paper is not the goal.
judges.strongest_objection: The two cleanest positive results in the evidence base both cut against compile-to-weights, and the idea cites one of them as support. Universal Computer's 59.5M model is perfect at 7,552 lines with the program in context and looked up by retrieval steps; that is arm C, not arm B. NLI scores 0.00/0.00/0.17 OOD when the program is inferred in a single amortized pass and 0.99/1.00/0.91 only with 100 gradient steps from 1024 restarts; the Stencil Tape compiler is exactly a single amortized pass on held-out rules. Add the researcher's own 0.0283 with the textbook in context on the checkpoint proposed as the stage-3 compiler. The evidence predicts C matches B at every k, which the idea itself defines as collapse to DNAR plus a persistent kernel.
judges.what_survives: The discrete-state, per-step-supervised, static-N tape executor as a throughput and bounded-space substrate (DNAR discreteness plus Persistent-RNN kernel discipline), and the k-sweep past k=4 on disjoint rules, which nobody has run. Promote arm C (rule enters by attention over the orbit or textbook at every sweep) to the main design and keep compile-to-weights as an ablation. Run A versus C first; if token CoT with stepwise targets also holds at k=128, the contribution is wall-clock and constant context rather than architecture, and that is still a real result on this benchmark. Fix scheduled sampling by re-running the reference implementation on the corrupted tape for targets. For stage 3, replace one-pass amortized compile with NLI-style test-time gradient search over the delta against a few reference traces, or with attend-over-textbook, and do not use the 350M checkpoint as a one-pass compiler until it clears its own 0.0283 in-context number. Drop the pbit claim or restate it with hidden units and multiple Gibbs sweeps per step.

judges.lens: TESTABILITY: can the killing experiment run for under $2,000 on one GPU by one person with the 350M checkpoint, the Coconut codebase, and the procedural generators, is the falsifier a number, and would a positive result be a breakthrough or a datapoint.
judges.verdict:
The 1dCA stage is runnable and cheap. Five arms times three seeds of a ~2M parameter executor on a width-20-to-64 tape is tens of L40S hours; arm A at k=128 and W=64 is an 8.8k-token sequence in a 4-layer d=128 model, which is fine. The $150-300 estimate is credible and the whole stage could nearly run on the M2 Pro. The wall-clock gate is also runnable: at B=1024, W=128, in=320, h=256, out=64 the two matmuls are about 26 GFLOP per sweep (the proposal says 10), which is 50 to 150 microseconds under CUDA graphs, so "under 200 us" is borderline but measurable. The problem is what the numbers would mean.

Three things make the result ambiguous as written. First, the kill thresholds (0.5 EM at k=8, per-cell error under 1e-3) ignore rule identifiability. With r=2 there are 32 rule entries and many CA rules collapse to fixed points or short cycles within a few steps, so a 10-state orbit often leaves entries unobserved; Kortical's "held-out rule entry" framing exists for this reason. At k=8 to 128 the trajectory visits neighborhoods the orbit never showed, and the gold answer is undetermined by the input. A perfect executor guessing those entries fails the 1e-3 test through no fault of the architecture, and a fail at k=8 cannot be attributed. The proposal never computes the Bayes-optimal ceiling per k, which is a one-day enumeration job. Second, the kill sits at k=8 and is absolute, while the claim is above 90% at k>=32 on held-out rules. B can survive its own kill at 0.55 while arm A scores 0.85 at the same k. Third, the demotion outcome is the expected one: on 1dCA the compiled program is 32 bits and arm C (each cell cross-attends to orbit transitions) is a one-hop pattern match that attention solves exactly, so C matching B is the likely result and by the proposal's own rule that collapses the architectural claim to DNAR-style discrete execution, which already extrapolates perfectly OOD on CLRS with argmax state and teacher forcing.

The stage where the breakthrough would live is the formal-systems stage, and that one is not specified well enough to run. I checked the researcher's repo: the Coconut codebase is a cross-model projector over a Z_10 compose task and ProsQA, not reusable here beyond a data loader. The invented-system generators (per the research export) verify answers by a reference implementation and emit chains of intermediate values for evaluate-x-OP-y problems; they do not emit tape states at sweep granularity, and a radius-r stencil with one d=32 global-read head cannot do an arithmetic rewrite in one sweep. Someone has to hand-design a tape encoding and a sweep-level trace emitter for every system class, which is the fully-supervised-trace requirement that killed NPI and which the proposal itself lists as prior failure. On top of that, the compiler must turn textbook prose into weights implementing a novel operator, when the researcher's own 350M scores 0.68 applying such an operator once with the textbook in front of it. The 50 to 100 H200 hours is a plausible GPU bill; the engineering is a month or more, not two to three weeks, and the outcome hinges on design choices the proposal has not made.

Positive result: on 1dCA a 2M executor plus hypernetwork hitting k=128 would read dramatically next to "below 0.25 at k=3," but the below-0.25 numbers come from models asked to fold k steps into fixed depth with no per-step state, so the comparison is between problem formulations, not architectures. Reviewers would call it a CA simulator with a learned lookup table. Datapoint. The hardware gate tests something not in doubt (a 2M MLP sweep is faster than a token decode).
judges.strongest_objection: The runnable stage cannot produce a breakthrough and the breakthrough stage cannot be run as written. On 1dCA at r=2 the per-problem "program" is a 32-bit lookup, the executor is a 5-input boolean function, and per-step discrete teacher-forced execution is already known to extrapolate (DNAR), so arm C attending to the orbit should match arm B and trigger the proposal's own demotion; the kill numbers are further contaminated by rules the 10-state orbit does not identify, which the proposal never measures. The formal-systems stage, the only place the 10^4-step claim lives, needs sweep-level tape traces the reference implementations do not produce and a hand-designed tape encoding per system class, which is exactly the NPI trace-supervision failure the proposal cites as prior art.
judges.what_survives: The B/C/D/E ablation on 1dCA is worth about $300 and answers a question the evidence base names and nobody has decomposed: whether per-step discretization, per-step supervision, or both are what let token execution extrapolate where latent recurrence dies at k~3. Run it with three amendments: enumerate all rules consistent with each orbit and report exact match against the Bayes-optimal ceiling (or restrict the test set to fully identified rules); move the kill to k=32 and make it relative to arm A rather than an absolute 0.5; drop the wall-clock gate, since a stencil sweep beating a token decode is not in question. If B beats D at large k and beats E everywhere, that is a clean mechanism result for the token/latent tension, publishable as a measurement even though it is not the architectural breakthrough claimed. For the compile-to-weights claim, use the researcher's existing chained Z_10 compose task as the first formal system: its intermediate values are already emitted, it has a natural one-value-cell tape with a pointer, and the "textbook" is an operator table, so the compiler test (350M emits a LoRA that the executor runs on an unseen operator table) becomes a week of work instead of a month and produces a real yes or no before anyone designs tape encodings for arithmetic rewrites.

idea.lens: Adversarial to the transformer: the transformer is a good parallel content-addressed reader and a bad serial machine, because its only carrier of state between serial steps is an analog residual stream (or an append-only token trace). Every system that executes long computations correctly (interpreter-trace transformers, PENCIL, Altabaa's discrete recurrence, DiscoLoop, token CoT) re-quantizes the state every step and writes it somewhere outside the residual stream. Every system that fails at k~4 (Coconut, looping, ARMT, ACT) carries state in the residual stream. So build the machine that the evidence already describes: demote the transformer to a stateless microcode ALU, and put all serial state in a bounded, integer-valued, overwritable register file.
idea.name: Digital Register Machine (DRM)
idea.one_sentence: Replace the transformer's analog residual carry with a small integer register file that a shallow attention ALU overwrites through hard-addressed writes and re-reads through the input embedding pathway each step, trained step-parallel on allocator-compiled interpreter traces so that step 10,000 is statistically identical to step 10 and a 50M-parameter machine executes unseen programs for thousands of steps with no tokens, no vocab head, and no BPTT.
idea.mechanism:
STATE. A register file M is an integer tensor of shape [R, c] with each entry in {0..L-1} (for example R=64 cells, c=16 lattice dims, L=8 levels: 48 bits per cell, about 3 kbit per problem), plus one control cell (program counter / phase) on the same lattice. Nothing else carries state across steps: no residual stream is fed back, no KV entry is appended. A fixed codec Enc maps any bounded-precision value (int, bool, symbol id, short tuple) to a lattice point digit-wise, and Dec inverts it exactly; a few extra lattice dims per cell are "free" (FSQ-quantized, no codec target) so the ALU can stash learned auxiliary state. Because the codec is fixed, any verifier or any other model can read the state.

READ. Each cell is embedded as e_r = W_e * onehot(M[r]) + slot_r, where W_e is the same embedding used for value literals in the program/problem context, and slot_r is one of R learned slot vectors. This is the manifold-matching step: a value sitting in a register looks to the ALU exactly like a value sitting in the input, so the rule-application circuit learned on inputs applies unchanged at every step. The program and problem are encoded once per request into a read-only KV cache that the ALU reaches only through cross-attention; program tokens never enter the register file (a Harvard split, motivated by the researcher's in-context 0.0283 vs retrieved 0.1233 anomaly).

ALU. A 2-4 layer transformer (d=256-512, ~5-50M params) runs over the fixed-length sequence [control, e_1..e_R] with cross-attention to the program cache. Its output is W write heads (W=2): each head emits address logits over R+1 (the extra index is NOP) and c softmaxes of L levels for the value. At inference: argmax address, argmax per dim, scatter into M. Shapes are static ([B, R+1, d] in, [B, W, R+1] and [B, W, c, L] out), so the whole step is one CUDA graph or one persistent megakernel; a fixed step budget T per request replaces halting (learned NOP writes fill the tail), matching the researcher's finding that depth must be static per request.

TRAINING SIGNAL. A reference interpreter runs random programs (the researcher's invented formal systems and mathgen, plus a MicroPy-style language) and a canonical linear-scan allocator compiles each interpreter step into (address, value) writes over R registers. Every training example is a tuple (M_t, program, writes_{t+1}); the loss is CE(address) + sum over dims CE(value level), with teacher forcing of M_t from the trace. All steps of all traces are independent samples, so training is as parallel as next-token prediction: zero backprop through time. With probability p a random cell of M_t is corrupted and the target write is unchanged, so the ALU learns restoration (Altabaa's error-correction trick, applied to a register file). For tasks with no trace, Dec lets the reference verifier score intermediate register states, giving a dense per-step reward.

HOW EACH DRAGON DIES.
1. Throughput (Neural GPU: sequential unfolded depth). Training has no unfolding at all (teacher-forced step tuples). Inference is a static-shape step over R+1 positions with no vocab projection, no sampling, no growing KV cache; the researcher's own H200 numbers (10% eager vs 34.8% CUDA-graphed) and Cohere's 1.58x batch-1 megakernel gain apply directly. One register write per step replaces the roughly 10-20 subword tokens of a trace line, so serial steps drop by about an order of magnitude versus token traces.
2. Addressing (soft addressing noisy and flat, exponential degradation on chained reads). Writes are hard-addressed, supervised by the allocator (no Gumbel needed), and every cell is re-snapped to the lattice on write, so a chain of 10,000 read-modify-writes accumulates zero analog error, for the same reason digital logic beat analog computers (signal restoration at every gate). Soft attention survives only inside a step, over R slots, at chain depth 1, which is exactly the regime where transformers are reliable (k=1: 0.95 in Beyond Memorization).
3. Credit assignment (NPI needed fully supervised traces). Traces are now free and unbounded: a reference interpreter plus a random program generator produce them, and the Universal Computer result (59.5M, random MicroPy traces, perfect on human-written programs at 60x length) shows random-program traces transfer. The researcher already owns reference implementations for invented systems. For trace-free tasks, Dec plus the verifier gives per-step reward, so a rollout that is right through step 6 earns credit for steps 1-6 and the reward_std -> 0 cold start cannot occur.
4. Generalization (fragile OOD). Step-count extrapolation is structural, not hoped for: no position index, no depth counter, no residual drift enters the ALU; the input distribution at step 10,000 is the input distribution at step 10, because the state is bounded and re-quantized. Ouro's degradation past trained depth and the looped-transformer ceiling are both residual-drift phenomena that cannot occur here. The only remaining OOD axis is value magnitude, which the digit-wise codec handles and which is tested separately.
idea.why_it_could_be_a_breakthrough: Today depth is paid for in serial tokens: Qwen3.5-4B burns ~240M output tokens for AA Index 20, and a 4B model keeps 92-101% of a 27B on knowledge benchmarks but 30-69% on depth benchmarks. If the DRM works, a ~50M ALU attached to a 1B-class model executes an in-context formal system for 10^4 serial steps at roughly a tenth of the serial steps of a token trace, with each step a static-shape kernel and no vocabulary softmax, and the machine's entire reasoning state is ~3 kbit of integers that any verifier can check and any other model can read. Three beliefs would change: that serial depth in small models must be bought with hundreds of millions of tokens; that latent reasoning is inherently capped near k~4; and that reasoning state must be an opaque residual stream (the researcher's own cross-model handoff, which needed a rank-8 adapter because "a frozen network cannot read another model's residual stream", becomes a digital register copy). It would also give RL a dense per-step signal from a formal verifier, which is the missing ingredient behind the researcher's 0.000 on multi-step composition across six objectives.
idea.evidence_that_generates_it: (1) Beyond Memorization: latent accuracy k=1 0.95, k=2 0.40, k>=3 below 0.25, and k=4 poor regardless of depth; token CoT with stepwise supervision >90% at k<=4 at ~1M params. Depth is not the limiter; the carrier of state is. (2) Ouro 1.4B: 41.21 -> 60.43 -> 66.71 -> 67.45 then degrades past trained depth; Saunshi: 1 layer x 8 loops equals 8 layers (73.2 vs 73.2) and stops. Both are what an analog residual carry predicts. (3) Universal Computer: 59.5M params, traces capped at 128 lines in training, perfect at 7,552 lines: an append-only discrete trace gives unbounded serial depth, so discrete externalized state is sufficient; the DRM keeps the discreteness and removes the append. (4) Transformers are Stateless DNCs: the two missing pieces are read-modify-write and persistent control state; the DRM adds exactly those two and nothing else. (5) The researcher's own numbers: 0.947 retrieval, 0.680 single-step rule application, 0.000 multi-step under RL (no substrate, no dense signal); in-context textbook 0.0283 with well-formedness 0.34 vs retrieved 0.1233 at 0.97 (program tokens in the stream compete with computation, hence the Harvard split); frozen receiver 0.268 vs rank-8 adapter 0.994 (residual streams are not a transferable state format). (6) H200 profiling: 10% utilization eager, 34.8% CUDA-graphed, data-dependent shapes cannot be graphed (hence fixed R, fixed W, fixed T, NOP writes, no halting). (7) FrogNano: synthetic tasks at the learnability frontier beat real data (1500 synthetic -> 61.5 vs 1500 real -> 53.4) and the GRPO cold-start trap (reward_std -> 0) hit four times in one day: trace synthesis and per-step reward are the task-side fix. (8) NLI: removing the discrete program takes 97% -> 1%; the discrete state is load-bearing. (9) PENCIL at 25M: bounded context with an erase token beats unbounded CoT, which is the append-vs-overwrite distinction.
idea.nearest_prior_art:
Searched ten phrasings via exa plus arXiv reads. Closest hits, honestly ranked:
1. Altabaa, Chen, Lafferty, Yang, "Unlocking OOD Generalization in Transformers via Recursive Latent Space Reasoning" (arXiv 2510.14095, Oct 2025). A 2-layer d=256 recurrent transformer; discrete bottleneck by per-factor argmax (syntax, variable id, value 0-22, op) and re-embedding; stepwise supervision on nodes of depth <= t; random corruption of discrete state for error correction; modular-arithmetic DAGs, train N<=32, test N=128; continuous latent supervision degrades gradually, discrete is much better, discrete plus error correction is near-perfect. This already shows discretization matters beyond supervision. Differences: their state lives in the input's own token positions (one per DAG node), so there is no allocation, no bounded memory, no overwrite of scratch, no loops; the codebook is task-specific symbolic factors; T is scaled by a graph depth known from the input.
2. Xu, Yang, Li, McAllester, "Training Transformers as a Universal Computer" (arXiv 2604.25166): token traces, 59.5M, 60x extrapolation. Append-only, subword-serial, vocab head.
3. "A Symbolic Neural CPU for Quantization-Simulated Writeback" (arXiv 2607.10021, Jul 2026): trace-supervised recurrent control, fixed differentiable ALU op bank, destination-masked register writeback, 1,000-instruction programs, 8-bit writeback preserves the op path; no learned ALU, no unseen-program generalization claim.
4. DiscoLoop (arXiv 2607.00341, Jul 2026): loops a discrete embedding channel alongside the continuous one; finds bridge entities are decodable but misaligned with token embeddings until re-embedded; two-hop only. LOTUS (arXiv 2606.31779): looped padded transformer with CE on each latent block's gold CoT token, closes the gap at 3B.
5. Robinson, "Progress Extrapolating Algorithmic Learning to Arbitrary Sequence Lengths" (arXiv 2003.08494): activation binning plus a digital loss and a localized memory to stop drift on copy/parentheses/addition.
6. Reflex (github ilbertt/reflex, Apr 2026): frozen LLM emits one RV32I instruction per cycle to a real CPU via cross-attention, output snapped to an instruction codebook so per-step noise cannot flip a bit.
7. "Quantizing Recursive Reasoning Models" (arXiv 2607.16237): 4-bit per-step error accumulates across recursion, Sudoku 84.1% -> 0.0%, direct evidence that unrestored recurrent state drifts.
8. "Do Language Models Need Sleep?" (arXiv 2605.26099): GDN fast weights on Rule 110 t-step prediction, ~10% -> ~30% at t=32 with sleep loops; fast weights alone do not buy serial depth, which is why the DRM does not use them.
9. NTM/DNC/NPI (2014-2016), Valdez's differentiable tensor computer (Aug 2026, everything soft), Percepta transformer-vm (analytic weights, no learning).
Nothing found combines a bounded overwritable register file with hard allocator-supervised addresses, a fixed value codec, step-parallel trace training, and a structural (not empirical) step-count extrapolation claim; and nobody has run the discrete-without-supervision arm or a head-to-head on the Beyond Memorization 1dCA setup.
idea.what_is_genuinely_new: Three things, stated without inflation. (a) The claim itself: the k~4 latent ceiling is a substrate property of analog residual carry, and the cure is not depth, recurrence, ACT, fast weights or more supervision but moving all serial state into a bounded, lattice-quantized, overwritable register file that is re-embedded through the input pathway every step; step-count extrapolation then follows by construction because no depth or position variable reaches the ALU. Altabaa's result is the strongest hint, but it is confined to input-position state on DAGs, and the discrete-without-stepwise-supervision arm has never been run. (b) The machine: learned dynamic allocation over R overwritable slots (supervised by a canonical allocator on random-program traces), a fixed digit-wise codec so the state is exactly decodable by verifiers and by other models (a digital handoff that removes the residual-stream projector problem in the researcher's own pipeline), a hybrid of codec dims and free FSQ dims per cell, a Harvard split between program cache and register file, and step-parallel training with zero BPTT. The Universal Computer has no overwrite and no bound; the Symbolic Neural CPU has no learned ALU and no unseen-program claim; NTM/DNC had soft addressing and BPTT. (c) The falsification design: a direct head-to-head against the published Beyond Memorization numbers, with a discrete-unsupervised arm that separates discretization from supervision, which is the untested half of the tension the brief names. What is not new: re-embedding discrete state (Altabaa, DiscoLoop), trace supervision (NPI, Universal Computer), corruption for error correction (Altabaa), FSQ (Mentzer 2023).
idea.killing_experiment:
Experiment 1 (about $30, one day on an L40S). Reproduce the Beyond Memorization 1dCA setup: 4-layer GPT-NeoX-style d=128, disjoint train/test rules, short state-sequence prompt, predict the state k steps ahead. Register file R = tape width, SIMD update (all cells written each step, so addressing is trivial and only the substrate is tested). Train on k<=4 with per-step CA states as targets, evaluate at k = 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. Four arms, same params and data: A) continuous recurrence with stepwise latent supervision through a linear probe (Altabaa's "continuous" arm); B) DRM: lattice-quantized cells re-embedded through the input embedding, stepwise supervision; C) DRM with final-answer supervision only (straight-through); D) token CoT with stepwise supervision (the published >90% at k<=4 baseline). The idea is dead if arm B trained on k<=4 scores below 0.90 at k=32, or if arm A matches arm B within noise at k>=8 (then discretization is unnecessary and the substrate claim is false). Arm C decides the tension: if C fails and B works, supervision is necessary but not sufficient; if C works, discretization alone extends depth.
Experiment 2 (about $600-1,000, one to two weeks on one H200). Compile the researcher's invented-system and mathgen interpreters plus a MicroPy-style language to (address, value) traces via a linear-scan allocator over R=64. Train a ~50M ALU on random programs with traces capped at 128 steps; test on held-out human-written programs (binary multiplication, SAT) at 1,000 to 8,000 steps, the same 60x extrapolation the Universal Computer paper reports, and train a 59.5M token-trace model on the same programs as the control. Dead if the DRM's per-step write accuracy is below about 0.9999 (so 7,552 steps cannot be sustained) or if it extrapolates worse than the token-trace control at matched training compute. A secondary kill: if the free FSQ dims or the Harvard split show no effect in ablation, drop them and report that the win, if any, is Altabaa's mechanism plus bounded overwrite.
idea.cost: Under $1,200 total on one GPU: about $30 for the 1dCA four-arm study (tiny models, hours), $600-1,000 for the 50M register-trace machine plus its 59.5M token-trace control at 60x extrapolation, and about $100 of slack for ablations (free dims, Harvard split, corruption rate). No new data collection: all traces come from generators and reference interpreters the researcher already owns. Fits the ~$4,700 budget with room for a follow-up that attaches the ALU to the 350M fact-free checkpoint.

judges.verdict:
Fifteen searches plus direct reads of five sources. The DRM's central claim and its machine both exist in print, and the arm the generator calls untested has a published negative result.

1. Discrete Neural Algorithmic Reasoning, Rodionov and Prokhorenkova, ICML 2025 (arXiv 2402.11628). Thesis: classical computation is a sequence of transitions between finite discrete states, so force the neural reasoner to keep its whole execution trajectory as finite predefined states. Mechanism: every cross-step state is a one-hot per node and edge, argmaxed and re-embedded each step; discrete and continuous flows are separated (the DRM's codec dims vs free dims); hard attention; teacher forcing on ground-truth states, which is step-parallel training with no BPTT. Result: perfect node-level and graph-level scores on BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, Prim, MIS from train size 16 to test size 1600, single-task and multitask, with a correctness proof for any input. Appendix A: the same processor without discrete bottlenecks falls to graph-level 0.0 at size 800 on BFS and at size 80 on DFS and Prim. Section 6 runs discrete state with no stepwise supervision (Gumbel-softmax over states): the best BFS model scores 99/86 at n=5, 94/34 at n=16, 79/0 at n=64, never reaches a perfect validation score, and fails at distances beyond those seen in training. That is Experiment 1 arm C, already answered.

2. anadim/subleq-transformer Round 2 (Papailiopoulos, GitHub, March 2026, paper.tex in the repo, no arXiv id found). A 4.9M encoder-only transformer trained from scratch on single-step SUBLEQ transitions: state is one PC plus 32 memory cells as 8-bit two's-complement integer tokens, re-embedded through the token embedding each step, argmax on output, fixed-shape loop, weighted CE with 100x on changed positions (write supervision), 60% random single-step pairs plus 40% consecutive trace pairs, zero BPTT. Results: 100% single-step on 3,682 held-out states; 99.8% over 804 multi-step programs including Fibonacci (47 steps), division (91 steps) and isqrt (61 steps) that never appeared in training in any form. This is a bounded, integer-valued, overwritable register file driven by a stateless transformer ALU, trained step-parallel on interpreter traces, executing unseen programs. Round 1 (hand-coded, 416 cells) also documents the failure the DRM must beat: 77.5% on random programs at 200 steps because per-step errors compound.

3. Altabaa et al. (arXiv 2510.14095) already report the continuous-vs-discrete comparison under identical stepwise supervision (Figure 4: Continuous Latent Space Supervision degrades with size, Discrete holds). Experiment 1 arm A vs B is a replication on a new task.

4. Further misses. ForgetNet (arXiv 2403.04929, ICLR 2024 spotlight) names and tests the Markov principle, no historical embeddings across steps, on CLRS-30. CLRS teacher-forced hint supervision (Velickovic et al. 2020 onward) is the step-parallel training recipe. Bansal et al. (arXiv 2202.05826) state the goal that the model must not learn behavior specific to iteration number and re-inject a read-only copy of the problem each iteration (the recall path, a cousin of the Harvard split). Discrete-Valued Neural Communication (arXiv 2107.02367) supplies the noise-robustness theory for discretized inter-step state. Debugging Code World Models (arXiv 2602.07672) shows a transformer propagates S5 permutation state over 128 teacher-forced swaps and that failures come from action generation, which is where the DRM's ALU sits. Loom (arXiv 2604.08816) and Percepta transformer-vm hold the entire machine state in a fixed-size tensor with fixed per-step cost, analytically. NRAM (arXiv 1511.06392) is the 2015 integer-register ancestor. Symbolic Neural CPU (arXiv 2607.10021) has destination-masked register writeback with trajectory supervision. Thinking States (arXiv 2602.08332) re-embeds discrete thought tokens, trains with teacher forcing, and extrapolates on state tracking.

5. A factual error in the proposal: the Universal Computer (arXiv 2604.25166) is not append-only. Its abstract and Section 3 say it uses PENCIL scaffolding to discard completed sub-computations inside a bounded context window. The append-vs-overwrite line the DRM draws against it does not hold as written.

Not found anywhere: a learned ALU that predicts address and value under an allocator-compiled trace for a language with variables and calls, with a NOP head and fixed step budget; a learned machine sustaining thousands of steps at per-step accuracy near 0.9999; a per-cell hybrid of codec dims and free FSQ dims; a 1dCA head-to-head against the Beyond Memorization numbers.
judges.strongest_objection: All three items the proposal lists as new are answered in print. The substrate claim is the thesis of Discrete Neural Algorithmic Reasoning (ICML 2025, arXiv 2402.11628), which forces every cross-step state into finite discrete symbols re-embedded each step, trains step-parallel with teacher forcing and no BPTT, reaches perfect generalization from size 16 to 1600 with a correctness proof, and whose ablations show the continuous carry collapsing to graph-level 0.0 and discrete-without-stepwise-supervision failing to generalize (79/0 at n=64). The machine exists as the learned SUBLEQ transformer (4.9M parameters, March 2026): integer memory cells re-embedded through the token embedding, argmax writeback, single-step-pair training, 99.8% on 804 unseen programs up to 91 steps. The falsification design's decisive arm has a published negative. Subtract those two, a linear-scan allocator, Bansal's recall path and Altabaa's corruption trick, and what is left is integration work, which is the recombination the researcher said they do not want.
judges.what_survives: Four pieces, none of them the headline. (1) Learned dynamic addressing: no one has trained a transformer to emit (address, value) writes over a bounded register file from allocator-compiled traces of a language with variables and procedure calls. SUBLEQ carries explicit addresses in the program and the Symbolic Neural CPU uses a fixed ALU bank. The allocator-supervised address head, the NOP write and the fixed step budget together are the one component without a direct precedent. (2) The depth number: the best learned discrete step machine on record runs 91 steps at 99.8% program accuracy and shows compounding by 200 steps. Sustaining 0.9999 per-step accuracy over 7,552 steps against a token-trace control at matched compute would be a real result, and it is a measurement rather than an architecture. (3) Experiment 1 as a replication: reproducing the Beyond Memorization 1dCA setup with a re-quantized, re-embedded state is worth the $30 as a check that the Discrete NAR and Altabaa findings transfer to that benchmark, but arm C should be framed as a replication of Discrete NAR Section 6, not as an untested question. (4) The digital handoff: a fixed-codec register file read by a second model as a state format, tied to the researcher's frozen-receiver 0.268 vs rank-8 adapter 0.994 result, has no match in the search. It is the only piece that connects to the researcher's existing pipeline instead of reproducing 2025 to 2026 work, and it is cheap.

judges.verdict:
No verified number kills the core mechanism, but the idea misreads three of its sources, overclaims "structural" extrapolation, and contains two components that cannot be trained as written. Checked item by item:

1. Beyond Memorization (verified from the full paper): tape width 20, radius 2 (32-entry rule table), accuracy is exact match of the whole 20-cell state, the rule is inferred from the state-sequence prompt, and every model is trained separately per k. The paper never tests extrapolation beyond trained k. So the "k~4 latent ceiling" is a fixed-k training result, not an extrapolation result, and Experiment 1 (train k<=4, test k=32 at >=0.90 whole-state exact match) has no baseline in the source, including for arm D. Token CoT at >90% for k=1..4 implies per-step whole-state accuracy of roughly 0.974 or better; 0.974^32 is 0.43. The k=1 baseline at 0.95 on the exact architecture Exp 1 reuses (4-layer d=128) is the best available estimate of the DRM's per-step rule-inference-plus-application accuracy, and 0.95^32 is 0.19. Reaching 0.90 at k=32 needs >=0.9967 per step. Nothing in the evidence shows that discretizing the carrier moves in-context rule application from 0.95 to 0.9967; discretization removes drift, not rule error. Worse, with a short prompt some of the 32 neighborhoods may never appear, so the rule is underdetermined and 0.90 at k=32 may be unreachable by any executor. Exp 1 needs an oracle-rule upper bound or its kill criterion cannot separate substrate failure from prompt underdetermination.

2. Universal Computer (59.5M, perfect at 7,552 lines): this is a fixed language whose semantics live in the weights; held-out programs are new compositions of known primitives. Exp 2 (invented-system interpreters plus a MicroPy-style language, trained on random programs) sits in this regime and is well supported. The breakthrough pitch ("executes an in-context formal system for 10^4 steps") slides into the unseen-rules regime, where the verified per-step numbers are 0.95 (1dCA k=1) and the researcher's own 0.680 single-step rule application. The idea conflates the two regimes. Also arithmetic: 0.9999 per step gives exp(-0.755) = 0.47 program success at 7,552 steps, so the stated kill threshold is 10x too loose; "perfect" needs about 0.99999.

3. Altabaa (verified): 2 layers, d=256, train N<=32, test N<=128 (4x), recurrent step count scales with graph depth read from the input, state lives at input token positions, and error correction works because a corrupted intermediate is recomputable from its parents, which persist at their positions. The idea transfers the corruption trick to a register file with a linear-scan allocator, where the parents may already be overwritten. Training "corrupt a cell, keep the target write unchanged" then teaches the ALU to ignore operands in favor of priors, which is the opposite of what an executor should learn. The continuous-vs-discrete comparison there does show supervision is not the whole story, but on a 4x extrapolation with adaptive T, not the 60x with fixed T the DRM claims "by construction."

4. Saunshi and Ouro are misread. 1 layer x 8 loops = 8 layers (73.2 vs 73.2) is looping reaching task-required depth, not an analog-drift ceiling; Ouro degrading past trained depth is what any model does outside its training depth. The generator says "both are what analog residual carry predicts," but so does "task saturates at depth d." These numbers do not discriminate and do not generate the idea.

5. "Step 10,000 is statistically identical to step 10" is false for any program with a counter or accumulator; with traces capped at 128 steps, a loop index at iteration 1,000 is out of distribution. Binary multiplication and SAT, the idea's own Exp 2 targets, both grow state. The digit-wise codec makes this plausible, not structural.

6. Mechanism incoherence: the free FSQ dims cannot be trained under the stated regime. Training tuples teacher-force M_t from the trace, which has no free dims, and there is no downstream step for a straight-through gradient to flow through. Either the free dims are dead or "zero BPTT" is false (a 2-step unroll is required). Also, "W_e is the same embedding used for value literals in the program" requires the program cache to be lattice-coded rather than subword text, which the "attach to a 1B model" pitch does not address.

7. Consistent or favorable: the Stateless DNC framing (adds read-modify-write and control state, nothing else) matches; fixed R, W, T and NOP writes match the H200 finding that depth must be static; PENCIL and the 0.268 vs 0.994 handoff numbers (verified in results/small_scale/RESULTS.md) support digital state as a transfer format; FrogNano's synthetic-task result supports trace synthesis. One correction to the evidence base: the "nobody has measured fast weights on serial depth" gap is stale. The sleep paper measured a 4-layer GDN-attention hybrid on Rule 110 at t=32 and got about 10% without offline loops, which supports the DRM's choice to avoid fast weights.
judges.strongest_objection: The DRM needs per-step whole-state accuracy of at least 0.9967 (Exp 1, k=32) and about 0.99999 (7,552 steps), and the only evidence for that reliability is the Universal Computer, where the language semantics are trained into the weights. In the in-context-rule regime that the idea sells as the breakthrough and that Exp 1 actually tests, the verified per-step numbers on the same architecture are 0.95 (Beyond Memorization, k=1, whole-state exact match on 20 cells, 4-layer d=128) and the researcher's own 0.680 single-step rule application. Lattice re-quantization eliminates analog drift, not rule-application error, and an overwrite machine has no redundancy to correct a wrong write (Altabaa's error correction depends on DAG parents persisting at their token positions). So Exp 1 will most likely miss 0.90 at k=32 for reasons that have nothing to do with the substrate, and the idea as written would misattribute that result. Beyond Memorization also never tested extrapolation beyond trained k (each model was trained per k), so the "k~4 latent ceiling" the DRM claims to cure is a fixed-k ceiling with no extrapolation baseline anywhere in the evidence.
judges.what_survives: Experiment 2 in the fixed-language regime: a bounded, overwritable, hard-addressed register file trained step-parallel on allocator-compiled interpreter traces, head-to-head against a token-trace control at matched compute and 60x length extrapolation. That is the genuinely untested piece (Universal Computer has no overwrite or bound, Altabaa has no allocation and a 4x adaptive-T extrapolation), it is cheap, and the Universal Computer number makes per-step reliability plausible there. Keep the Harvard split and the fixed codec as ablations. Repair before running: (1) drop the free FSQ dims or add a 2-step unroll with straight-through, and say so; (2) restrict corruption to cells whose value is recomputable from live registers, or corrupt and change the target to a re-derivation; (3) set the per-step kill at about 0.99999, not 0.9999; (4) in Exp 1, add an oracle-rule symbolic executor as the upper bound and define the kill relative to it, and train and evaluate arm D at k=32 too, since the source never extrapolated; (5) stop citing Saunshi and Ouro as evidence of analog drift. Arm C (discrete, final-answer supervision only) remains the one experiment that adds information beyond Altabaa, and the fast-weight exclusion is now supported by the Rule 110 result rather than by a gap.

judges.verdict:
Cost in dollars is credible; cost in person-time and the sharpness of the kill are not. Experiment 1 is cheap: the source paper trained its 4-layer d=128 baseline for 40k steps at batch 256 on 9.5e5 instances on a single RTX 6000 Ada, so four arms with a few seeds is $50-150 on an L40S, not $30, but close enough. Experiment 2 is under-budgeted in time, not money: it needs a linear-scan allocator compiling three interpreter languages to (address, value) writes, an ALU with cross-attention to a program cache and two write heads, a closed-loop harness for 8,000-step runs, and a from-scratch replication of the Universal Computer paper's 60x length extrapolation as the control. That is five to nine weeks for one person, not one to two. Nothing in this repo helps beyond the training loop: /Users/pyro/multi-model-latent-space-reasoning/src/compose.py is a single-register Z_10 chain with no trace emitter, src/coconut.py is continuous feedback (arm A material at best), and the invented-system and mathgen generators with reference implementations are not in this repo or anywhere obvious on this machine, so their step-level trace output is unverified. The 350M checkpoint is unused by both experiments.

The falsifier has numbers (0.90 exact match at k=32; 0.9999 per-step write accuracy), which puts it ahead of most proposals, but the first number is attached to a task with an uncontrolled ceiling (see the objection), and the four-arm design cannot isolate the variable it claims to isolate. Arm A has no continuous ground-truth state, so it must be trained by BPTT through k steps; arm B is teacher-forced with zero BPTT. Substrate and training regime change together, which is inherent: discretization is what makes teacher forcing possible, so "is supervision the whole story" is not a question this 2x2 can answer. Arm C (discrete, final-answer only) needs straight-through gradients through four quantized steps; its failure reads as an optimization failure as easily as a capacity failure, and the proposal interprets it as the latter. The source paper also already reports an intermediate-state supervision variant (O-O) that gave no gain without token CoT, and Altabaa 2510.14095 already reports continuous-supervised latent state degrading where discrete re-embedded state holds, so arm A versus arm B is a replication on a new task.

A positive result is a datapoint. Exp 1 positive: Altabaa's discretization result on 1dCA plus step-count extrapolation of a teacher-forced discrete machine, which the Universal Computer paper already shows for append-only traces. Exp 2 positive: a register-format interpreter that runs at ~10x fewer serial steps than a token trace, an efficiency and format result. Neither experiment tests the breakthrough claim (a 1B-class model using the ALU to reason), and neither touches the k~4 ceiling as measured, because both hand the machine a compiled program and an allocator-supervised trace; the Beyond Memorization ceiling is about inducing and composing rules the model was not given. NPI with unlimited free traces would pass the same tests. Exp 2 also compares a 3 kbit bounded state against an append-only trace with unbounded lookback on SAT, so a DRM loss there could be memory capacity rather than substrate, and a control that fails to reproduce the paper's perfect-at-7,552 result makes the comparison uninformative.
judges.strongest_objection: The kill number for Experiment 1 (arm B below 0.90 exact match at k=32) is pinned to a task whose best achievable score is unknown and plausibly below 0.90. In the Beyond Memorization setup the model must infer a radius-2 rule (32-entry table, 4.3e9 rule space) from a 10-state orbit of width 20 and is scored by exact match on the full 20-bit state. A 10-state orbit exposes at most 180 neighborhood-to-output transitions and can leave rule entries unobserved; a 32-step closed-loop trajectory will visit neighborhoods the prompt never showed, and under a chaotic rule one wrong cell destroys exact match within a few steps. The paper's own k=1 score is 0.95, so the threshold leaves five points for 32 steps of compounding plus an uncomputed induction ceiling. The experiment can therefore kill a correct serial-substrate hypothesis for a reason belonging to the transformer's parallel reading job (rule underdetermination), which is the opposite of what it claims to test, and no oracle-ceiling or explicit-rule control is specified.
judges.what_survives: Three pieces, all cheaper than what was proposed. First, run the substrate test with the rule given explicitly in a read-only program cache (this is the DRM's own Harvard split, so it is not a concession): train on single-step teacher-forced tuples, measure per-cell and per-state single-step accuracy on held-out rules, then closed-loop exact match at k = 32, 256, 1024, for arm A (BPTT, probe-supervised) and arm B (teacher-forced discrete). Report an oracle ceiling from a symbolic rule inducer if the original orbit prompt is kept as a secondary comparison. The sharp kill is per-state per-step accuracy on held-out rules below 0.999 (0.999^32 = 0.97; the k=1024 extrapolation claim needs about 0.9999), measurable in one day for about $30. Second, keep the 0.9999 per-step write accuracy threshold but move it to the first day of Experiment 2, measured under teacher forcing on held-out programs, before any closed-loop harness or control is built. Third, shrink Experiment 2 to the one question that separates the DRM from Altabaa: does learned hard addressing over a bounded overwritable file (R=16, a hand-written allocator, one tiny language extending the existing compose task to named registers) generalize to unseen programs at 10x training length, against an in-house token-trace control on the same language, not a replication of the Universal Computer at 60x. That costs a few hundred dollars and two weeks. Drop the claim that a positive result changes beliefs about the k~4 latent ceiling; state it as trace-supervised register execution extrapolating in step count at a fraction of the serial steps of a token trace.

idea.lens: Separation of concerns, pushed to the limit: the language model never takes a reasoning step, the executor never sees a word, and nothing crosses between them except a compiled program (as weights) and a discrete state tape.
idea.name: Airlock
idea.one_sentence: A 350M language model writes a discrete rule table and an initial state once, a deterministic loader compiles the rule table into the weights of a ~20M executor that never sees language, the executor rewrites a discrete state tape in parallel for k steps with its residual stream wiped between steps, and the language model reads the final tape once; the interface is weights plus a register file, not tokens and not a shared residual stream.
idea.mechanism:
Three components, no shared parameters, no shared vocabulary, no gradient across the boundary.

1. The tape. A fixed-schema register file S_t in {0..V-1}^{W x F}: W cells, F small fields per cell (symbol, pointer, flag, halt). It is not drawn from the LM vocabulary. Cells hold pointers as hard addresses (cell indices), which gives the executor exact dereference instead of soft content addressing.

2. The executor E (about 10-20M params: 6 layers, d=256, attention over the W cells). Each step: embed S_t fresh (a new residual stream every step, no hidden state carried over), run L layers, emit per-cell per-field logits, argmax, write S_{t+1}. One of the layers is the rule layer, and its weights are not learned per problem; they are set by a deterministic loader from a discrete rule table R. For lookup-table rules (1dCA, wide-neighborhood CA, arithmetic tables) the loader writes W_rule[pattern] = onehot(output). For pattern/template rewrite rules the loader writes one key-value pair per rule (K = encoded LHS pattern, V = encoded RHS template) into a hard-selection attention layer (argmax over rules, straight-through in training). The rest of E's weights are slow weights trained once across random rule sets so that any loaded rule layer works. A halt field freezes the tape: once set, E is trained to be the identity, so the executor runs a static K steps inside one CUDA graph (the researcher measured that data-dependent depth cannot be graphed).

Training signal for E: the researcher's procedural generators sample rule sets R and initial states S_0; the reference implementation produces S_1..S_k. Loss = sum over t of per-cell per-field cross-entropy between E(S_t; loader(R)) and S_{t+1}, teacher-forced on true S_t, with a scheduled fraction of self-rollouts so E learns to be robust to its own rare errors. Test rule sets are disjoint from training (the Beyond Memorization protocol). Where the reference allows it, S_{t+1} is the maximally parallel step (all non-conflicting rule applications at once), so serial cost is the critical path of the derivation, not its trace length.

3. The language model (the 350M fact-free checkpoint, later MiniCPM5-1B). It gets two small heads and nothing else: a tape-writer (linear map from hidden states at designated slot positions to per-cell per-field logits for R and S_0) and a tape-reader (an embedding table from tape symbols into the LM input at designated positions for S_K). It is trained by supervised learning on generator pairs: (NL textbook + problem statement) -> (R, S_0) and (S_K + question) -> NL answer. It is a transliterator. It never applies a rule.

Test-time selection. The LM samples N candidate rule tables R_1..R_N. For each, the executor is run for ONE step on a handful of random states s, giving f_i(s). The LM is asked, in language, for its own one-step prediction g(s) (the researcher's model already does this at 0.68). The table with the highest agreement with g over the sampled states is loaded. This uses single-step competence, which exists, to pick the program, and hands composition, which does not exist in the LM, to the executor. Optional last stage: GRPO over the transliteration with the frozen executor and the reference verifier as reward, with generator difficulty knobs set to a target resolve rate near 0.5 so reward_std stays away from zero (the cold-start trap the researcher hit four times).

Inference: one LM forward (write), loader, K graphed executor passes, one LM forward (read). No output tokens are generated during execution.
idea.why_it_could_be_a_breakthrough: If it works, serial depth is decoupled from both parameter count and output-token count, which are the two things every number in the evidence base says depth is currently paid in. A 350M model plus a 20M sidecar would perform exact k=64 composition on formal systems it has never seen, described in natural language, in 64 forward passes of a 20M network (on the order of 10-20 ms graphed), where the same 350M model scores 0.000 at k=2 and a distilled 4B reasoner would spend thousands of serial output tokens. The 4B versus 27B gap on depth benchmarks would no longer be a fact about model size for any task that reduces to rule execution over a formal state; the 4B would keep its knowledge-shaped 92-101% retention and buy depth for free. It would also settle the open tension: Altabaa et al. already show supervision is not the whole story (continuous supervised latents degrade OOD, discrete ones do not). Airlock adds the third separation, program out of context, and if that arm wins over program-in-context at large rule sets and large k, the explanation of k~4 becomes: soft state, program tokens competing with computation, and language sharing the executor's weights, each independently fatal and each independently removable. On-device consequences: MiniCPM5-1B class hosts would gain a deterministic, verifiable, graphable reasoning coprocessor whose procedures live at about one bit per weight by construction.
idea.evidence_that_generates_it: Textbook in context 0.0283 with well-formedness collapsing to 0.34 versus retrieved 0.1233 at 0.97: program tokens in the LM's residual stream compete with computation, so the program must never be in a context that also computes; here it enters as weights. Xu et al. 59.5M perfect at 7,552 trace lines (60x extrapolation) with plain next-token prediction: a network that never predicts English executes perfectly, so the executor should be a separate network. Beyond Memorization k=1 0.95, k=2 0.40, k>=3 below 0.25, ARMT to k=2 only, ACT +1 step, depth sweep does not help: rule inference works and chaining in soft state fails, so chaining must move to discrete state. ~1M-param token CoT above 90% at k<=4 on the same task: discrete supervised state chains. Ouro 41/60/67/67 then degrading past trained depth, and Saunshi 1 layer x 8 loops = 8 layers and stops: soft recurrence has a ceiling equal to its unrolled depth. The researcher's 0.9474 retrieval, 0.680 single-step, 0.000 multi-step across six RL objectives: single-step competence exists and is the resource the selection stage spends; composition does not exist and is never asked of the LM. The DNC theorem (write-once memory, no persistent control state): the tape is read-modify-write and carries control state as cells. NTM/DNC soft addressing degrading exponentially on chained reads: pointers are hard cell indices and rule dispatch is argmax. NLI 97% -> 1% without the discrete program: the program is a discrete table. Fast-weight gap (nobody has measured serial depth) and MIX-STQ (content survives at 1.31 bits, never tried for procedures): the rule layer is a one-shot weight load at about one bit per weight, so the experiment measures both. Qwen3.5-4B ~240M output tokens for AA Index 20: output tokens are the serial cost; Airlock generates none during execution. H200 profiling: recurrence graphs only at static depth, so the halt-freeze design with fixed K. FrogNano's task calibration at resolve rate 0.5 and the four cold-start traps: the optional RL stage calibrates on generator difficulty.
idea.nearest_prior_art:
Searched nine phrasings via exa and fetched six papers. Honest map:
(1) Altabaa, Chen, Lafferty, Yang, arXiv 2510.14095 (Yale, 2025): input-adaptive recurrence + per-step latent supervision + discrete bottleneck (argmax over four symbolic factors, re-embed) + error correction on modular arithmetic over DAGs; trained N<=32, tested N=128; continuous latent supervision "slowly degrades" OOD, discrete gives near-perfect OOD. This already answers the evidence base's "is supervision the whole story" question with no, for their task. Airlock's discrete tape is the same move; that part is not new.
(2) Rodionov and Prokhorenkova, Discrete Neural Algorithmic Reasoning, ICML 2025: finite predefined states with transition supervision, perfect OOD on CLRS; GNN, algorithm fixed in weights, no program supplied at test time.
(3) Xu, Yang, Li, McAllester, arXiv 2604.25166: learned universal interpreter, program in context, autoregressive small-step traces with PENCIL scaffolding (bounded context already handled).
(4) Reflex (github.com/ilbertt/reflex, Apr 2026): frozen Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with gated cross-attention over 65 machine-state tokens emits one RV32I instruction per cycle via cosine snap to a 691-row codebook; 34/41 tasks, 199 consecutive correct instructions at ~97% per-step. The LM is in the loop every cycle and the executor is a real CPU.
(5) Loom, arXiv 2604.08816: analytical looped transformer executing compiled C with the full machine state in a fixed tensor, snapping to {-1,+1} to kill drift, 4.7M params, no learning; Percepta transformer-vm does the same for WASM.
(6) Neural Stored-program Memory (1906.08862) and Neurocoder (ICML 2022): controller weights fetched from memory, learned, NTM-style tasks; the closest thing to program-as-loaded-weights.
(7) LOTUS, Fan, Svete, Lee, arXiv 2606.31779: looped padded transformer with parallel supervision on gold CoT tokens matches explicit CoT at 3B; continuous latents, no depth-generalization claim.
(8) Compile by Training, Deng, Nie, Shieber, arXiv 2609.04199 (5 days old): LLM generates examples that train a local adapter; the interface is a gradient, 83.6% on FuzzyBench-Hard.
(9) NLI (2604.18907), PAL (ICML 2023), HINT/Text-to-LoRA hypernetworks, Neural GPU, Burtsev's ECA transformers, AutomataGPT (98.5% one-step on unseen 2D CA rules).
Nothing found combines: LM out of the loop (write once, read once), program compiled into a learned executor's weights rather than placed in context, parallel discrete tape with a wiped residual, and program selection by agreement with the LM's own single-step judgments.
idea.what_is_genuinely_new: Four things, stated narrowly because the field is crowded. First, the program crosses the boundary as weights: an LM-emitted discrete rule table is compiled by a deterministic loader into a hot-swappable rule layer of a learned executor whose slow weights were trained across random rule sets; Xu and Reflex keep the program in context or feed it per cycle, Loom and transformer-vm are hand-built and unlearned, NSM learns its stored programs. Second, the LM is entirely out of the loop: one write, one read, zero LM forward passes during execution, versus Reflex's one 7B pass per instruction. Third, composition is obtained from single-step competence without the LM composing: candidate rule tables are selected by agreement with the LM's one-step predictions, which converts a 0.68 knowledge-shaped skill into a depth-unbounded capability the LM measured at 0.000. Fourth, it is the first design that directly tests the two flagged gaps at once: whether a weight-resident procedure (a fast weight written once) extends serial depth, and whether procedures survive at about one bit per weight; the third-separation ablation (program in weights versus program in context, at matched executor and supervision) is a new question that Altabaa and Discrete NAR could not ask because their programs are fixed.
idea.killing_experiment:
Stage 1 (under $30). Reproduce the Beyond Memorization 1dCA protocol with disjoint train/test rules and a 4-layer d=128 executor. Arm A: rule table compiled into the lookup layer, discrete tape, wiped residual, per-step supervision. Arm B: identical but the rule table is given as context tokens. Arm C: identical to A but continuous state (no argmax, per-step linear-probe supervision). Evaluate at k = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 with the rule table inferred by a small network from the short state prefix (their k=1 result of 0.95 says this is learnable). Kill condition 1: Arm A below 0.9 at k=8 kills the whole idea (the separations do not extend depth on the canonical task). Kill condition 2: Arm B equal to Arm A across k and across rule-set sizes (8, 64, 512 rules) kills the program-as-weights claim; what remains is Altabaa plus Xu and the idea should be abandoned as a recombination. Arm C at or above Arm A kills the discreteness claim for this task.

Stage 2 (under $100). Same three arms on the researcher's invented formal systems with the reference implementation supplying maximally parallel traces, rule sets held out, k to 32.

Stage 3 (under $300). Attach the 350M model: transliteration accuracy from textbook to rule table, then full pipeline accuracy at k = 1..8 against two baselines: the researcher's 0.000, and the LM applied step by step with context erasure (expected 0.68^k, 0.21 at k=4). Kill condition 3: pipeline at k=4 not clearly above 0.21 means the airlock bought nothing over letting the LM take erased single steps, and the idea is dead as a system even if the executor works in isolation.
idea.cost: About $300-600 of the $2,000 ceiling. Stage 1: 1dCA executors at ~1M params, roughly 3-5 GPU-hours on an L40S, under $30. Stage 2: 10-20M executors on generator traces, 10-20 GPU-hours, under $100. Stage 3: 350M SFT for the tape heads plus pipeline evaluation, 10-15 H200-hours, roughly $60; optional calibrated GRPO through the frozen executor, 40-60 H200-hours, roughly $200-250. All static-depth executor runs fit in CUDA graphs, and every stage uses the existing generators, reference implementations, and the Coconut codebase's slot-feeding machinery for the tape heads.

judges.verdict:
Each of the four "genuinely new" claims has a published instance the generator missed, and one of them is a name-level hit.

1. "The program crosses the boundary as weights; the LM is invoked once and never re-enters the loop." This is Program-as-Weights, arXiv 2607.02512 (Zhang, Hotsko, Kim, Nie, Shieber, Deng, July 2026): a 4B compiler reads a natural-language spec once and emits a discrete pseudo-program plus a LoRA adapter for a frozen 0.6B interpreter; the paper's own framing is "invoked once per function definition ... a small reusable artifact." The generator cited its follow-up (Compile by Training, 2609.04199) but not PAW itself. TeNet, arXiv 2601.15912, does the same for control: LLM text embedding -> hypernetwork -> a compact policy that runs with no LLM present, "using the language only once at policy instantiation time." HINT (2212.10315), Text-to-LoRA (ICML 2025, 2506.06105), Doc-to-LoRA and SHINE (2602.06358) all move a task description out of context and into weights. The deterministic loader that compiles a discrete program into executor weights is Adaptive Neural Compilation (NeurIPS 2016, arXiv 1605.07969), which compiles low-level programs into the weights of a differentiable machine.

2. "Composition from single-step competence: select candidate rule tables by agreement with the LM's own one-step predictions on sampled states." This is SYNTRA, Program Synthesis via Test-Time Transduction (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2509.17393): "we use an LLM to predict outputs for selected test inputs and eliminate inconsistent hypotheses," with a greedy maximin choice of which inputs to query. LLM-PV (2510.14331), Oracle-Guided Program Selection (ISSTA 2024), functional clustering (2506.11021) and Semantic Voting (2605.08680) are the same move with different aggregation rules. Swapping a Python interpreter for a learned executor does not change the method.

3. "Discrete tape, wiped residual, per-step supervision, hard pointers." The generator already concedes Altabaa et al. (2510.14095) and Discrete NAR (ICML 2025). Add Emergent Discrete Controller Modules (ICLR 2026, Rafiuddin and Khan): registers, flags, memory and a Gumbel-softmax primitive selector inside transformer blocks with length generalization; and the Symbolic Neural CPU (2607.10021), trace-supervised with destination-masked register writeback through 1000-instruction programs.

4. "First direct test of whether a weight-resident procedure extends serial depth, and whether procedures survive at one bit per weight." Serial composition in fast-weight models is measured at length in the state-tracking literature: Merrill's Illusion of State (ICML 2024), Grazzi et al. (ICLR 2025 oral, 2411.12537) on DeltaNet parity and modular counting, Siems et al. (2602.14814) on permutation composition from code traces. Not on 1dCA, but the "nobody has measured" framing is wrong. DiffLogic CA (2506.04912) already runs CA rules as binary logic gates, discrete at inference, so procedures at one bit per weight exist. Meta-Tool (2604.20148) is a direct negative on the weights-versus-context question: a 227.8M hypernetwork producing LoRA weights for a 3B model added 0% over few-shot prompting.

What is left after subtraction is one ablation: at matched executor, matched supervision and disjoint rules, does putting the rule table in a lookup layer instead of in the executor's context change k-step accuracy as rule-set size grows. That is a measurement, and the researcher said they do not want a measurement paper.
judges.strongest_objection: The one component that is not already published is orthogonal to the depth result it is supposed to explain. For a 1dCA lookup rule, W_rule[pattern] = onehot(output) is an embedding lookup; an executor with the eight rule entries in context performs the identical lookup with one attention head, and Xu et al. and Turing Programs (2407.03310) show program-in-context executors already length-generalize. Neither placement touches the mechanism that would carry k to 32, which is the discrete tape with per-step supervision, and that mechanism is Altabaa plus Discrete NAR. So if Arm A reaches 0.9 at k=8, the credit goes to prior art, and the only new arm (A versus B) has a published negative (Meta-Tool, 0% gain from hypernetwork weights over prompting) and a functional-equivalence argument against it. The researcher's own in-context anomaly (0.0283 vs 0.1233) came from a 350M model that both holds the program and computes; it says nothing about a 20M executor that never sees language, so it does not predict the ablation either. The design is PAW's compiler-plus-frozen-interpreter, SYNTRA's oracle selection, and Altabaa's discrete recurrence, assembled around Rodkin et al.'s benchmark.
